After mid-exponential phase, most cells possess multiple protrusions of uniform diameter (approximately 370 nm), varying lengths, branching and bulbous expansions (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), morphologically similar to P. syntrophicum MK-D13,4 and ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5. Based on observations using scanning EM (SEM), protrusions were absent in all cells that appear to be undergoing cell division (cells that are in the middle of separating into two cocci with characteristic rings in both cocci marking where cell division probably began; Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3e), suggesting that protrusion generation and cell division are mutually exclusive processes. The protrusions often comprised more than half the volume of each cell (roughly 1.7 µm3 or 142% of the main cell body, on average; Supplementary Table 3), suggesting they have an important role in the physiology of these archaea. Notably, both protrusions and cells were flexible and were observed to sway by Brownian motion (Supplementary Videos 3 and 4). We found that fixation with formaldehyde tended to disconnect their protrusions (Supplementary Fig. 5), indicating that caution must be taken in defining morphology using fixed cells. The protrusions of all isolated and highly enriched Promethearchaeota3,4,5 were observed to physically attach to syntrophic partners. For HC1 and SC1, helical filaments on the protrusion surface tended to be found at the protrusion–partner interface (Fig. 2d,e, Extended Data Figs. 2e,f and 3g–j and Supplementary Note 7). Given the consistent presence of protrusions in Promethearchaeota cultures, we suspect that LAECA also probably possessed such structures.

We further microscopically investigated whether these Hodarchaeales strains have a complex eukaryote-like internal system. The eukaryote endomembrane system is characterized with universally conserved, physically persistent organelles (the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum) and structurally transient compartments (such as Golgi apparatus and lysosomes), all integrated by regulated membrane trafficking. Based on transmission EM (TEM) and cryo-EM, we did not observe any persistent internal membrane structures shared among all HC1 or SC1 cells (Fig. 2g,h,k,l, Extended Data Figs. 2h–j and 3k,l,t,u,w and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Meanwhile, although infrequent, low-electron-density intracellular vesicle-like structures were observed in some cells (Fig. 2m,n, Extended Data Fig. 3m,n,v and Supplementary Video 1). This indicates the absence of persistent eukaryote-like organelles and presence of transient internal structures. Consistent with this, a Heimdallarchaeales archaeon (‘Candidatus Yibarchaeum umbracryptum’) enriched by a recent study lacked persistent organelles and possessed transient intracellular vesicles of unknown function that appeared during early growth stages40. With current data, it is unclear whether the transient structures are related to ESPs, a primitive endomembrane system, or neither.

Despite the absence of conserved internal membrane structures, nearly all HC1 and SC1 cells showed spatial separation between DNA and rRNA based on fluorescence microscopy using DAPI and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (Fig. 2i, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Video 5), as also previously observed in other Promethearchaeia and Heimdallarchaeia41,42. The reason for this spatial localization is not yet clear, but histones may mediate DNA compaction43. All microscopically studied Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeales—albeit three strains only—consistently lack conserved, persistent eukaryote-like organelles. Despite this cell architecture, HC1 and SC1 have a comparable number of ESPs associated with endosomal sorting and trafficking (11 and 10 out of 34 types) to other Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeia (10 ± 2 and 10 ± 2 types on average, respectively) (Supplementary Table 7). These suggest that other extant Heimdallarchaeia may also lack persistent internal structures. Given that only 9 out of 34 of the endosomal sorting and trafficking-related ESP types are moderately conserved across Heimdallarchaeia (found in at least 50% of the genomes associated with each order), LAECA may have also possessed few such ESPs. Although this suggests the possibility that LAECA also lacked persistent internal cell structure, the genomic composition of LAECA remains to be resolved.

The HC1 co-culture and SC1 tri-culture both contain H2-using methanogenic archaea, and addition of the methanogenesis inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate (10 mM) to the cultures completely suppressed growth. This shows that both HC1 and SC1 depend on H2-mediated symbiosis with methanogens. Such a metabolic symbiosis is known as syntrophy, in which an organotroph performs a hydrogen and/or formate-yielding metabolism that is thermodynamically inhibited by these products and a partner organism scavenges these products to low non-inhibitory concentrations44. Accordingly, amending high concentrations of hydrogen gas or formate also suppressed the growth of both strains (Supplementary Table 9). In the SC1 tri-culture, we detected a methanogen that uses only methylated compounds, Methanolobus sp. MLB, and suspect that SC1 may generate methanol through formate reduction through the expressed aldehyde reductase and alcohol dehydrogenase (Supplementary Table 6), a recently discovered pathway and phenomenon45. Given that syntrophy and symbiosis have been hypothesized to be relevant to the origin of eukaryotes4,12,23, the identification of these features in Heimadallarchaeia has major evolutionary implications.

Both strains are clearly dependent on peptides, as supplementation with non-proteinaceous substrates did not stimulate growth of HC1 and SC1, and neither strain could grow when peptide substrates were replaced with a mixture of 20 proteinogenic amino acids (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 9). Ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC)-based analysis of macromolecule distributions in the cultures indicated clear consumption of higher-molecular-mass molecules (Fig. 3b,c, Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Note 8). Genome analyses revealed that both strains encode extracellular peptidases, peptide transporters, amino acid degradation pathways of glutamate, aspartate, threonine, methionine, glycine, serine, alanine and cysteine in both strains, and NiFe hydrogenases for syntrophic peptide degradation (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Energy is conserved through ATP synthesis through substrate-level phosphorylation and proton motive force generation coupled with ferredoxin-driven H2 generation (Fig. 4). Transcriptomic and proteomic data further confirmed their expression (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Glycoproteomics revealed that peptide/nickel transport system substrate-binding proteins of both strains were highly N-glycosylated like P. syntrophicum MK-D146 (Extended Data Fig. 8, Supplementary Table 8 and Supplementary Note 10), further evidencing the importance of peptides for the growth of these strains. Collectively, we demonstrate that both strains are obligately syntrophy-dependent peptidotrophic archaea.

In cultures of HC1, we observed that an increasing amount of peptides added to the medium increased the cell size and protrusion number but not the growth rate—a trend that is atypical of prokaryotes9. When the yeast extract concentration in the HC1 culture was increased from 0.005% to 0.05%, the growth rate (doubling times from 7 days to 6 days) did not significantly change (Fig. 1c). By contrast, observation of cells showed significant increases in the volume of the main cell body (from 1.2 ± 0.01 to 2.6 ± 0.01 µm3 estimated based on cell diameter increase from 1.3 ± 0.3 to 1.7 ± 0.3 µm; P = 1.3 × 10−24) (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 3). We further used wide-area SEM to analyse roughly 15,000 cells for changes in protrusion and vesicle production (Supplementary Fig. 7). We observed consistent increases, on a per-cell basis, in the volume and maximum number of protrusions (1.7 to 4.1 µm3 and 8 to 11, respectively), the volume and number of vesicles (0.02 to 0.11 µm3 and 0.4 to 3.7, respectively) and protein content (66 to 226 fg; Supplementary Table 10). Similar trends were observed for P. syntrophicum MK-D1 and SC1 (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 11 and Supplementary Note 11).

Collectively, these findings suggest that, when more carbon and energy are available, these strains allocate them primarily to the cell (that is, main cell body and protrusions) rather than to cell division. This is in direct contrast to typical prokaryotes that allocate available carbon and energy to the cell body and cell division and analogous to the biology of eukaryotes, for which size and reproduction rates are inversely related9,47,48. Although much more research is necessary to connect the cell biology and ESPs in Promethearchaeota with eukaryogenesis, we suspect from these results that Promethearchaeota’s unique aprokaryotic focus on cell maintenance/construction of membrane-based structures over growth may have served as a foundation for the evolution of elaborate membrane or cytoskeletal structures in its descendants that evolved towards eukaryotes. Potentially related to this, for all three Promethearchaeota strains, only non-dividing cells produce complex actin-containing protrusions, which are a major contributor to cell size (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3). As the number and volumes of protrusions increase when more carbon and energy are available and the protrusions are never observed in dividing cells, we suspect that, besides syntrophy, the protrusions and their contents (including actin filaments) may also serve as nutrient, energy and building block storage for later cell division. For example, in eukaryotes, it has long been known that muscle cells—more specifically, proteins abundant in these cells (such as actin and myosin)—function as reservoirs of amino acids49. Although tempting to speculate, it remains unclear whether these physiological functions are evolutionarily related.

The purified HC1 co-cultures showed no growth in culture medium containing trace levels of oxygen either (1) left by omission of reducing agents or (2) further added by supplementing the head space with gas containing 1% (v/v) oxygen. Both resulted in major decreases (roughly two orders of magnitude) in HC1 cell densities (Fig. 3a). However, for reducing-agent-free cultures, we found that HC1 could grow when aerobic bacteria were present—that is, Alcanivorax sp. AC and Mariniphaga sp. PC isolated from HC1 enrichment cultures (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 12). Nevertheless, HC1 cell yields did not increase. This indicates that HC1 is not stimulated by oxygen but can tolerate continuous exposure to oxygen when aerobic organisms are present and scavenging oxygen.

HC1 encodes and expresses pathways coupling anaerobic amino acid degradation with H2 generation (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). These pathways rely on NAD+, NADP+, ferredoxin and quinone as electron carriers and are fundamentally centred on ferredoxin-dependent electron transfer. We identified oxidoreductases that may facilitate electron transfer between these carriers, including NAD+:quinone and ferredoxin + NAD+:2NADP+ (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). These can ultimately funnel reducing equivalents to H2 or formate generation through membrane-bound and cytosolic NiFe hydrogenases and cytosolic formate dehydrogenase.

In contrast to hydrogenases found in MK-D1 and ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’, those encoded by HC1 are potentially aerotolerant, based on homology to archaeal hydrogenases that can tolerate short exposure to oxygen: MBH (group 4g) and SHI (group 3b)50,51 (catalytic subunit sequence identities of 45% and 49%). These observations suggest that HC1’s syntrophic anaerobic metabolism can tolerate low concentrations of oxygen while remaining fundamentally ferredoxin centred, a hallmark of anaerobic energy metabolism.

HC1 possesses genes encoding terminal oxidases—cytochrome bd oxidase (Cbd)-like protein and Cox—and expresses them despite the reduced anoxic culture conditions. While aerobic organisms possess a full set of enzymes for funnelling electrons from electron donors to quinones or cytochrome c, such pathways are absent in HC1 (Fig. 4). Even if we assumed the presence of an uncharacterized redox protein with quinone:cytochrome c oxidoreductase activity like cytochrome bc1, only part of the electrons derived from amino acid degradation would be transferrable to oxygen. As such, HC1 lacks the capacity to completely couple peptide degradation and oxygen respiration.

Previous studies, together with our genomic survey (Supplementary Table 13), show that strict anaerobes can use Cbd and/or Cox for scavenging and tolerating nanomolar to micromolar concentrations of oxygen rather than for respiration or growth52,53,54,55. Gene expressivity (translation efficiency) predicted from codon use56 also supported our interpretation that oxygen reduction is a supplementary function in HC1 physiology (Supplementary Table 5).

As a metabolic link between peptidotrophy and aerotolerance, we identified expression of oxygen-dependent enzymes for degradation of aromatic amino acids—phenylalanine, tryptophan and tyrosine57,58 (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 14). While these enzymes can participate in pathways that convert these amino acids to central metabolites (for example, fumarate, acetyl-CoA and alanine), HC1 possesses truncated pathways that neither conserve energy nor generate intermediates feeding into other metabolic processes. Such pathways can also be found in genera containing obligate anaerobes, such as Pyrobaculum, Thermoproteus, Thermovibrio and Desulfurobacterium. We therefore suspect that HC1 uses aromatic amino acids and these pathways to scavenge oxygen.

Moreover, the HC1 genome also encodes oxygen-tolerant central metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase) and oxidative stress enzymes (that is, catalase, superoxide dismutase, thioredoxin-dependent peroxiredoxin, peroxiredoxin 2/4, glutaredoxin-dependent peroxiredoxin, and globin; Supplementary Table 5). In HC1 cultures, we also verified the presence of haem B (Supplementary Fig. 8), a cofactor for catalase and superoxide dismutase. HC1 also possesses and expresses genes encoding proteins (such as xanthine dehydrogenase; Xdh) for the production of the antioxidant uric acid from purines—an oxidative-stress-mitigation strategy59. Ferritin, a key protein for reducing reactive oxygen species generation from the interaction of iron and oxygen60, was also among the three most expressed proteins in HC1’s transcriptome.

As with oxygen reduction, HC1 possesses a nitrate reductase homologous to respiratory nitrate reductase NarGHI but lacks pathways for funnelling all electrons from peptidotrophy to nitrate reduction (Supplementary Table 5). In HC1 and methanogen co-cultures supplemented with nitrate, we observed nitrate reduction activity and associated nitrite accumulation, but no stimulation of growth (Extended Data Fig. 10a). As predicted from the genome, only a small proportion of the electrons derived from peptide degradation (around 15%) were funnelled into nitrate reduction and the rest were transferred to the partner methanogen. Moreover, nitrate-amended cultures showed no growth when a methanogen inhibitor was present, indicating that HC1 strictly depends on syntrophy even when performing nitrate respiration. Given that nitrate (1 mM) is inhibitory (Extended Data Fig. 10b), we suspect the nitrate reductase may serve to scavenge nitrate rather than support nitrate-respiration-driven growth. This is analogous to the terminal oxidase-supported aerotolerance discussed above (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

We further evaluate whether the Promethearchaeota phylum broadly conserves anaerobic lifestyles regardless of the presence or absence of Cox, as observed in cultured representatives. One distinguishing metabolic feature between aerobes and anaerobes is dependency on oxygen-sensitive 4Fe–4S ferredoxin-dependent enzymes and alternative oxygen-tolerant NAD-dependent enzymes in central metabolism: 2-oxoacid:ferredoxin oxidoreductases (OFORs) and 2-oxoacid dehydrogenases (ODHs). Oxidation or reductive generation of 2-oxoacids occurs repeatedly across multiple central metabolic pathways, including pyruvate oxidation/synthesis, the citric acid cycle and amino acid metabolism, with distinct enzymes acting on specific 2-oxoacids or sets of 2-oxoacids. Thus, the relative genomic representation of OFORs and ODHs should reflect the extent to which an organism relies on anaerobic ferredoxin-dependent metabolism versus oxygen-tolerant NAD-dependent metabolism. For example, the obligate aerobe Bacillus subtilis lacks OFOR and possesses four core E1 dehydrogenase subunits of ODH to support organics degradation and assimilation, whereas the obligate anaerobe Methanocaldococcus jannaschii lacks ODH but encodes two OFORs to support pyruvate synthesis and a partial reductive TCA cycle for autotrophic growth. We therefore propose abundances of these proteins as a metric for examining whether an organism may be capable or incapable of aerobic growth. The abundances of OFOR and ODH homologues in each isolate normalized to genome size clearly separate obligate anaerobes (with and without Cox) from obligate and facultative aerobes (Fig. 5a–c and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16). A binary classifier trained on these features achieved high accuracy with consistent results across models (balanced accuracies of 0.96 and 0.95 using logistic regression (LR) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA); Supplementary Tables 16) and accurately classified obligate anaerobes that encode Cox (accuracy of 0.97 using LR). This indicates that comparison of OFOR and ODH abundance provides a robust discriminator of metabolic lifestyle.

Heimdallarchaeia (Heimdall.) and other Promethearchaeota genomes are shown as diamonds and circles, respectively. Strain HC1 and Heimdallarchaeia MAGs encoding Cox are indicated (pink and black diamonds, respectively). b,c, Pairwise Euclidean distances (b) and Mahalanobis distances (c) between category centroids in the OFOR–ODH feature space. Strain HC1, other Heimdallarchaeia MAGs encoding Cox and those without Cox are indicated (pink, black and grey diamonds, respectively). While recently proposed approaches for aerobe–anaerobe classification show comparable overall accuracy32,61,62, they exhibited lower predictive capacities for obligate anaerobes that encode Cox compared with the OFOR–ODH-based classifier, falsely classifying some as aerobes (accuracies of 0.9 and 0.76; Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 16). For the classifier based on aerobe–anaerobe-associated genes62, the inclusion and predominance of terminal-oxidase-related genes (that is, terminal oxidase subunits and biosynthesis proteins for terminal oxidase haem groups) in the top contributing genes for aerobe prediction may have contributed to the false predictions. Thus, although the presence of Cox is often implemented as an indicator for potential for aerobiosis, cultivation and comparative genomics here indicate that caution must be taken in interpreting the physiology of Cox-containing organisms, including those of Heimdallarchaeia.

Promethearchaeota, including HC1 and other recently reported Cox-encoding Heimdallarchaeia31,32, exhibit OFOR–ODH abundances similar to anaerobic isolates (Fig. 5a–d). Applying the OFOR–ODH-based classifiers, all the analysed genomes of Heimdallarchaeia were consistently predicted to be anaerobic with high confidence regardless of the presence or absence of Cox (mean maximum posterior probabilities of 0.98 ± 0.04 and 0.97 ± 0.06 for LR and LDA; Supplementary Tables 16 and 17). Nearly all other Promethearchaeota genomes were also confidently classified as anaerobic. Classification based on aerobe–anaerobe-associated genes62 also predicted most Cox-encoding Heimdallarchaeia, including HC1, as anaerobic (maximum posterior probabilities of 0.97 ± 0.12 and 0.96 ± 0.09 for LR and LDA, for those predicted as anaerobes). For lineages encoding Cox, this pattern suggests that terminal oxidases are more likely to function in aerotolerance rather than supporting canonical aerobic respiration. We illustrate the ferredoxin-centric metabolisms of HC1 in Fig. 4.

A specific comparison of Promethearchaeota with other archaea yielded a similar pattern. Although archaea capable of aerobic growth often retain ferredoxin-dependent metabolism despite exposure to O2, their OFOR repertoires were genomically distinct from those of obligate anaerobes. Nearly all aerobic isolates (334 out of 340 isolates, or 97%) encoded OFOR containing the POR, POR_N and PFOR_II domains that accounted for more than one-third of their OFORs, whereas, for obligately anaerobic isolates, this OFOR represented no more than one-third of their OFORs (Supplementary Table 18). All analysed Heimdallarchaeia also showed low relative abundances of this aerobe-associated OFOR. Accordingly, their abundances of other OFORs and ODHs were distinct from those of aerobic archaea and instead similar to those of obligately anaerobic archaea and bacteria (Fig. 5d).

Although a recent metagenomic survey proposed aerobic lifestyles for Hodarchaeales based on occurrence of Cox-harbouring MAGs in oxic environments including pelagic habitats (for example, epi-, bathy- and hadal-pelagic)32, all such MAGs were derived from sediments (that is, benthic), where oxygen exposure is highly ambiguous given that concentrations typically decline sharply below the surface63. Moreover, Hodarchaeales were detected in public metagenomic datasets annotated as derived from oxygen-associated environments32, but the presence of oxygen is unclear given that these are sediment samples or oxygen concentrations are either below the detection limit or not measured.

Consistent with this, most Promethearchaeota species—including HC1 and Cox-containing Heimdallarchaeia—have oxygen-sensitive NiFe hydrogenases, reflecting dependence on anaerobic metabolism. Promethearchaeota nearly universally possess group 3c and/or 4g hydrogenases (Supplementary Table 19). In Heimdallarchaeia, the orders Heimdallarchaeales, Gerdarchaeales and Hodarchaeales each generally conserve group 4g (92%), 3b/3c/4g (92%/80%/80%) and 3c (90%) hydrogenases, respectively (Supplementary Table 20). The widespread conservation of ferredoxin-oxidizing hydrogenases (groups 3c and 4g) further supports reliance on a ferredoxin-centred, anaerobic metabolic strategy across Promethearchaeota, including Heimdallarchaeia. Analysis of computed gene expressivity across all archaeal species representatives in GTDB release 220 suggests that anaerobic peptidotrophy is also widely conserved across Promethearchaeota (Fig. 3f, Methods, Supplementary Table 21 and Supplementary Note 12). The coupling of the two would implicate anaerobic H2-evolving peptidotrophy as a widely conserved feature of Promethearchaeota, which agrees with our previous hypothesis4 and phylogenetic analyses tracing organotrophic H2 production and acetogenesis through the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway to the Promethearchaeota ancestor7,64.

Given this broadly anaerobic metabolic framework, we next considered when these archaea may have acquired Cox-mediated aerotolerance. Phylogenetic analyses of the Cox complex based on a concatenated alignment (Cox1–3), Cox1 and Cox3 all show Heimdallarchaeales sequences nested within those of Hodarchaeales (Fig. 5e–g and Supplementary Fig. 10c–e). These topologies do not show evidence for the presence of Cox at the common ancestor of Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeales and suggest that Heimdallarchaeales acquired Cox horizontally from Hodarchaeales.

Here we isolated two strains from the archaeal lineage that descended from the last common ancestor of archaea and eukaryotes—Heimdallarchaeia—and reveal insights into their biology. Anaerobiosis, the absence of persistent intracellular structures and membrane protrusions are conserved among all cultured members, P. syntrophicum MK-D13,4, ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5, ‘Ca. N. marumarumayae’26, strains HC1 and SC1, and a recent Heimdallarchaeaceae enrichment culture40. Dependence on peptides and syntrophy for energy metabolism is also consistent across those with detailed physiological characterization3,5. These organisms further exhibit symbiotic, protrusion-mediated intercellular attachment, linking cell morphology with syntrophic interactions. The conservation of these physiological features across strains spanning two Promethearchaeota classes points towards an anaerobic, peptide-degrading and H2-evolving LAECA that lacked persistent internal structures but possessed membrane-based protrusions.

Consistent with this, members of the phylum, including all cultured strains, lack many pathways for biosynthesis of amino acids, vitamins and nucleotides (Supplementary Table 22), indicating metabolic dependence on partner organisms. Moreover, slow growth is also conserved across all cultured strains and, if LAECA also shared this feature, it may have contributed to key processes in eukaryogenesis (Supplementary Note 13). Although it is unclear whether LAECA possessed Cox, cultivation and comparative genomics indicate that Cox in Heimdallarchaeia are unlikely to function in oxygen respiration. Together, these observations suggest that the prokaryote–eukaryote transition may have involved a physiological shift from an anaerobic to (facultatively) aerobic lifestyle10, alongside major structural innovations. If LAECA was anaerobic but possessed aerotolerance like HC1 (and potentially other Heimdallarchaeia), this feature could have supported interaction with a mitochondrial ancestor under low-oxygen or fluctuating redox conditions, where oxygen reduction by the bacterial partner may have alleviated oxygen toxicity. This relationship is also consistent with the ‘Ox–Tox’ model positing that the mitochondrial progenitor had a role in oxygen detoxification for an anaerobic host65.

Although the extremely small cell size and slow growth rate of P. syntrophicum MK-D1, the only publicly available Promethearchaeota strain3,4, had posed a major obstacle, efforts in cultivation here led to the isolation of two strains that have larger cell sizes, higher growth rates, shorter lag phases and a closer relationship to eukaryotes. These make the strains promising model organisms for exploring the biology of Promethearchaeota that can catalyse investigations of cellular and physiological transitions underlying the emergence of eukaryotic complexity.

The biofilm samples were collected from a gas production well, KTG3, in the Southern Kanto gas field (Chiba Prefecture, Japan). The biofilm was located on a wall of the separator discharge outlet at a depth of 20–40 cm below the water surface. Samples were taken after eruption of brine on 29 August 2019, 16 July 2020 and 11 May 2023 (Extended Data Fig. 1). The gas field is located in an old marine forearc basin and is based on subsurface gas reservoirs in turbidite sandstones, making it geologically and geochemically relevant to past seawater and marine sediment66. The brine from the well KTG3 is rich in organic matter, iodine and iron. Detailed site information has been described previously37 and geochemical characteristics of the brine in the well KTG3 are provided in Extended Data Fig. 1b. The collected biofilm sample was placed in a 100 ml glass bottle filled with brine (no head space) and brought back to our laboratory under refrigerated conditions. The samples were also inoculated in 50 ml glass vials containing anaerobic medium onsite (Supplementary Note 2). Our iTag analysis showed that the biofilm contained abundant and diverse microorganisms, mostly affiliated with uncultured or cultivation-limited microbial groups, including Promethearchaeota. To isolate new Promethearchaeota strains from the samples, we used a strategic batch-type cultivation35 that incorporated previous knowledge and our expectations for this archaeal group (Supplementary Note 1). Detailed information about the cultivation, including the medium composition and purity checks for the HC1 and SC1 cultures, is provided in the Supplementary Methods. Unless otherwise indicated, the HC1 and SC1 cultures were grown in casamino acids–peptone–yeast extract medium (each at 0.005%, w/v) and casamino acids–powdered milk–polypeptone peptone–yeast extract medium (each at 0.005%, 0.005%, 0.01% and 0.05%, w/v), respectively, with an inoculum size of 16% (v/v) for HC1 and 20% (v/v) for SC1. To measure the dissolved oxygen concentrations in KTG3 culture medium lacking reducing agents, we used a fibre optic oxygen meter (Fibox 3 trace, Presence) in combination with an oxygen sensor (SP-PSt6-YAU). The SP-PSt6-YAU sensor was affixed to the inner wall of the 50 ml serum glass bottles using oxygen-permeable silicone adhesive.

DNA extraction, PCR mixture preparation and quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis were performed as described previously4,67. PCR primers for qPCR used in this study were designed using the probe design tool of ARB program68. The specificity of new primers was confirmed using BLAST and the ARB-SILVA database (https://www.arb-silva.de/)69. The primers and PCR conditions are shown in Supplementary Table 23. The doubling times of cultured archaea were calculated based on the semilogarithmic plot of the qPCR data. For iTag analysis, a universal primer pair 530F/907R, which contained overhang adapters at 5′ ends, was used70. The procedures used for library construction, sequencing and data analysis were described previously4. All samples for data acquisition were checked for growth and microbial composition by qPCR and iTag before or after the experiments.

To evaluate the temperature range for growth, a pure co-culture of HC1 and a tri-culture of SC1 were incubated at a range of 10 °C to 45 °C or 10 °C to 50 °C. All incubations were performed in triplicate. After a certain period of incubation, 16S rRNA gene copy numbers of each strain were evaluated by qPCR.

To examine substrate use of the cultured archaeal strains, the basal media were supplemented with each substrate sterilized either by autoclaving or filtration. We performed two successive transfers under the same cultivation conditions and conducted qPCR targeting the archaeal strains’ 16S rRNA genes in both the first and second subcultures. All incubations were performed in duplicates at the optimum growth temperature for each strain.

To assess the effect of non-proteinaceous substrates on growth of archaeal strains, we added individual substrates to culture medium containing casamino acids–peptone–yeast extract for HC1 and casamino acids–powdered milk–polypeptone peptone–yeast extract for SC1. Each cultivation condition was performed in duplicate.

An epifluorescence microscope (BX53, EVIDENT) equipped with a phase-contrast objective lens and a colour CCD camera system (DP80 or DP75, EVIDENT) was used for routine microscopy observation, with image acquisition and recording performed using cellSense v.4.3 (EVIDENT). When it was necessary to obtain images without cell movement due to Brownian motion, agarose-coated glass slides were used71. Cell and protrusion diameters of HC1 were measured from phase-contrast images using Fiji, an image analysis software based on ImageJ72.

For SEM analysis, archaeal cells were fixed by adding 2.5% (w/v) glutaraldehyde and incubating for 2 h under anoxic conditions at their optimum growth temperatures and then overnight at 4 °C. The sample preparation procedure was performed as described previously3. The samples were observed under an extreme-high-resolution focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM (Helios G4 UX, Thermo Fisher Scientific) system operated at 1 kV.

To evaluate the volumes and numbers of HC1 cell bodies, protrusions and membrane vesicles under different yeast extract concentrations, we acquired wide-area SEM images using Maps v.2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), which was installed in the FIB-SEM operation system. Wide-area images were obtained by stitching 100 images into a larger 10 × 10 image, with each image taken with an acceleration voltage of 1 kV, a beam current of 13 pA, a field of view of 36.3 µm × 24.2 µm and an image resolution of 23.6 nm per pixel. The acquired wide-area SEM images were then analysed using AMIRA 3D Pro 2024.1 and 2024.2 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). First, the images were denoised by applying curvature-driven diffusion73. Next, HC1 cell bodies, protrusions, membrane vesicles and Methanocalculus cells were segmented with the aid of a deep-learning module based on PyTorch74 and Keras (https://github.com/fchollet/keras). The deep learning model created from 2,000 × 2,000 pixels was adapted to the full images, followed by manual modification and watershed segmentation. Each segmented component, except for protrusions, was labelled and the area and perimeter were analysed. Protrusions were skeletonized using the Auto Skeleton module75, and the number of fibre segments and their curved length were measured after excluding looped fibres or those shorter than 10 pixels.

For the preparation of ultrathin sections of archaeal cells for TEM, we followed a previously established protocol3. The section samples were observed using a conventional TEM (Tecnai 20, FEI) system at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. Detailed information about observations of HC1’s membrane vesicles and thin filaments on the surface of SC1 protrusions is described in the Supplementary Methods.

For QFDE-EM observations, archaeal cultures (440 ml of HC1 culture and 25 ml of SC1 culture) were concentrated to approximately 5 ml through filtration using a 0.22-µm-pore-size polyethersulfone (PES) filter unit (Corning) and transferred to a glass vial in an anaerobic chamber (95:5 (v/v) N2:H2 atmosphere; COY Laboratory Products). To remove the H2, which is inhibitory to the strains, this vial’s headspace was replaced with N2/CO2 gas (80:20, v/v) through flushing. The subsequent procedure was performed as described previously3,76.

Before EM observation, 2 ml of culture liquid was taken from a culture bottle using a syringe, and the culture liquid was concentrated to approximately 50 µl by centrifugation at 20,400g for 10 min at 20 °C. Then, 3 µl of the concentrated liquid culture was applied onto a glow-discharged Quantifoil Mo grid R2/1 (Quantifoil MicroTools) after mixing with 15 nm gold colloids (Electron Microscopy Sciences) and plunge-frozen into liquid ethane using the Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 4 °C and 95% humidity. The frozen grids were screened on a 626 side-entry cryoholder (Gatan) with a 200 kV JEM2200FS electron microscope (JEOL). Suitable grids were processed for cryo-ET in the 300 kV Titan Krios G4 electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a bottom-mounted Selectris X energy filter (slit width, 5 eV) and a Falcon 4i direct detector camera. Tile series of each specimen were collected at a nominal magnification of ×19,500, resulting in an image resolution of 6.19 Å per pixel, and a dose symmetric tile scheme was performed between +60° and −60° at 2° increments using Tomography software implemented on a TITAN Krios G4, resulting in a total electron dose of 91.5 electrons per Å2. The tilt series was aligned with gold fiducials, and tomograms were reconstructed using filtered back projection or SIRT in the IMOD software77 with an image binning of 5. Segmentations of HC1’s cellular components were performed using AMIRA 3D Pro software. Cellular membranes and granular structures were segmented manually with the help of a deep-learning module, and actin filaments were segmented manually.

Cryo-EM images and tomograms shown in Extended Data Fig. 2i–n and Supplementary Video 2 were acquired using the CRYO ARM 300 II (JEOL) system. Detailed procedures for sample preparation and imaging conditions are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

The protocol for antibody preparation and observation by immunofluorescence for lokiactin generally followed that of a previous study5. The lokiactin antibodies were made using peptides specific for the lokiactin sequences of HC1 and SC1 (Supplementary Fig. 3). The regions of the peptides are the same region as the peptides for ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5. We made three antibodies in total (that is, ab1 for HC1; ab1 for SC1; and ab2 for both strains), and all of them were created using the service of Cosmo Bio and validated by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Detailed procedures of western blotting and immunofluorescence staining are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Cells were fixed under anoxic conditions by adding paraformaldehyde solution (methanol-free, formaldehyde solution, 16% (w/v), Electron Microscopy Sciences) to a final concentration of 4% (v/v) directly into the culture bottles and incubating for 2–3 h at 4 °C. After fixation, cells were washed with PBS (153.8 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM Na2HPO4, 1.5 mM KH2PO4 (pH 7.2)). Subsequently, cells were stored in 50% ethanol with PBS at −30 °C until use in subsequent experiments. The design of specific probes and hybridization chain reaction (HCR)-FISH were performed in accordance with previously described protocols4,78. A list of the 16S rRNA-targeted oligonucleotide probes used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 24. Cells were counterstained with DAPI in the ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant with DAPI (Thermo Fisher Scientific). FISH images were acquired using a STELLARIS STED confocal microscope (Leica) with a ×100/1.4 NA oil-immersion or ×93/1.3 NA glycerol-immersion objective lens at ×2 or ×6 zoom, a line-scanning frequency of 400 or 700 Hz and a line average of 3. Fluorescence signals were detected in confocal mode at 405, 499 and 553 nm for excitation, and some images were deconvolved using the adaptive Lightning strategy in LasX software (Leica) when necessary. The 3D video was constructed from 27 sections of 8.17 μm thick using the LasX software. Line-intensity profiles were obtained using LasX software for each of the DAPI and Alexa Fluor 488 channels along a line through the centre of the target cell.

To measure peptides and proteins, culture liquid samples were filtered through a 0.2 µm pore-size polytetrafluoroethylene filter unit (Merck Millipore) before sample preservation and analysis. The molecular mass distribution of peptides and proteins was determined using an UPLC system equipped with the ACQUITY UPLC Protein BEH SEV column (Waters) as described previously79.

Methane concentrations in the headspace of culture bottles were measured by gas chromatography as described previously4.

Measurement of haem B was performed according to the previously reported method80. For this measurement, archaeal cultures (440 ml of HC1, and 900 ml of P. syntrophicum MK-D1) were first concentrated to about 5 ml using a 0.22-µm-pore-size PES filter unit (Corning) on a clean bench. The concentrated cell suspensions were then further concentrated by pelleting the cells through centrifugation at 20,400g for 10 min at 4 °C. The collected cells were washed twice with their respective basal medium without energy substrates.

Nitrate and nitrite concentrations were measured by high-performance liquid chromatography (LC) using the TSKgel SAX column (Tosoh, 35 mm × 4.6 mm inner diameter) with 3% (w/v) NaCl as the eluent. The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, and detection was performed using a UV-VIS detector (GL-7451, GL Science) as described previously81.

Iron concentrations in the brine were determined by quadrupole inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS; iCAP Qc, Thermo Fisher Scientific). To prevent metal precipitation before measuring the total iron concentrations, brine samples were acidified with high-purity concentrated HNO3 (TAMAPURE AA-100, Tama Chemical) at a final concentration of 1.5 M. For ICP-MS analysis, the water sample was diluted with 0.3 M HNO3, and four internal standards (Be, Sc, Y and In) were added to correct instrument drift. Mass interferences were eliminated using the kinetic energy discrimination mode with H2 reaction gas for high-sensitivity 56Fe analysis.

Genomic DNA from HC1 and SC1 was extracted according to a previous protocol67. Whole-genome sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq system, with additional mate-pair sequencing for HC1 and Oxford Nanopore PromethION sequencing for SC1. Detailed procedures of genome assembly, gene prediction and functional annotation are described in the Supplementary Methods.

For RNA-based sequencing analysis, total RNA was extracted from HC1 and SC1 cells collected during their exponential growth phase. Specifically, cells were collected from a 25 ml HC1 culture grown for 25 days and a 50 ml SC1 culture grown for 51 days. To concentrate the cells, the cultures were first filtered through a 0.22-µm-pore-size PES filter unit (Corning) on a clean bench, reducing the volume to approximately 4 ml, and then centrifuged at 20,400g for 10 min at 4 °C for further concentration. Derailed procedures of RNA extraction, RNA-seq library preparation, sequencing and quantification of gene expression are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

For proteomic analysis, HC1, SC1 and P. syntrophicum MK-D1 were cultured under the conditions described in the Supplementary Methods. After confirming growth by qPCR, cells were concentrated using a PES filter unit followed by centrifugation, as done for the samples used in western blotting analysis. The collected cell samples were washed once with the basal medium lacking energy substrates, then suspended in 200 µl of 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (pH 8.6) containing 2 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride. Cells were disrupted by sonication at 2 °C using a Q700 sonicator (QSonica) operating at 40 kHz. The protein concentration of the cell-free extract was determined by a Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All subsequent procedures, including LC–tandem MS (LC–MS/MS) data acquisitions and data analysis, were performed as described previously82,83.

Glycoproteome analysis was performed using the same culture samples as those used for proteome analysis. The procedure was identical up to the point of cell disruption by sonication, after which half of the protein extract samples were allocated for glycoproteome analysis. Subsequent sample preparation, LC–MS/MS analysis and data processing were performed as previously described46,84.

ESPs in Promethearchaeota genomes were annotated using HMMER v.3.4 (hmmsearch)85 and HMM profiles are available from InterPro86. Hits were determined based on an e-value cut-off of 0.0001 and a bit score above the gathering threshold (GA) specified in each HMM profile. Distant hits were identified based on less stringent thresholds for e value (0.01) and bit score (GA-10). We annotated homologues of elongation factor 2 and DNA polymerase epsilon based on (1) distant homology with PFAM domains found in eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (PF00679, PF14492 and/or PF03764) and DNA polymerase epsilon (PF00136 and PF03104); (2) alignment using MAFFT (v.7.525; default options)87 with representatives of bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic homologues annotated with the above domains in UniProtKB (release 2026_01)88 and clustered with 60% sequence identity (MMseqs2 v.17.b804f)89; (3) trimming with trimAl (v.1.5.0; -gt 0.1)90; (4) tree construction with FastTree (v.2.1.11; -lg)91; and (5) identification of Promethearchaeota homologues that form a sister group with eukaryotic sequences

Promethearchaeota genomes were collected from the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) release 22092 and GenBank. Genomes not included in GTDB r220 were classified into species-level lineages defined in GTDB or new species based on sequence distances estimated using MASH (v.2.3)93. Coding sequences were predicted using Prokka (v.1.14.6)94 with the default parameters and annotated with eggnog-mapper (v.2.1.12)95 and the eggnog (v.5.0) database using the default parameters96. For constructing a genome-based phylogeny of Promethearchaeota, the following single-copy marker genes defined by GTDB were used for phylogenetic tree construction (Supplementary Table 25). Maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny was performed using IQTREE v.2.3.5 with ultrafast bootstrapping97, a concatenated alignment of these marker genes trimmed using BMGE v.1.12 (-m BLOSUM30 -g 0.67 -b 3)98 and a universal distribution model (UDM0064 LCLR) as previously described99. Maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny for the 16S rRNA gene was performed using a sequence alignment generated with MAFFT (--maxiterate 1000 --localpair)87, the optimum model selected by ModelFinder (SYM + R6)100 and regular bootstrapping. Bootstrap values were recalculated using BOOSTER (v.0.1.2)101.

For maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny of target genes, we first collected relevant sequences by using amino acid sequences obtained from Promethearchaeota as the query and searching against genes belonging to the same protein family collected from GTDB r220 species representatives92. For this, the MMseqs2 v.16.747c6 search command102 was used with three iterative searches with different sensitivities from sensitivity level 4 to 8.5 (--min-seq-id 0.3 -c 0.7). To select representative sequences for tree construction, we (1) clustered the collected sequences using the MMseqs2 cluster command102 (--min-seq-id 0.6 -c 0.7); (2) constructed a rough tree using FastTreeMP (v.2.1.11)91 with an alignment generated with MAFFT (v.7.525)87 and trimmed with trimAl v.1.5.0 (-gt 0.1)90; and (3) subsampled phylogenetically representative sequences from the tree using Parnas (v.0.1.6)103. An alignment for the representatives was generated using MAFFT-DASH (--localpair --maxiterate 100 --dash)104 and trimmed using trimAl (-gt 0.3). Finally, we used this as an input for maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny using IQTREE v.3.1.1 with either 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates or 100 bootstrap replicates97, and used ModelFinder100 to identify the best-fitting model among C10, C20, C30, C40, C50 and C60 (LG + CXX + G + F). For bootstrap replicates, transfer bootstrap expectation values were also calculated using BOOSTER (v.0.1.2)101.

For estimation of the phylogeny of the Cox complex, we used a concatenated alignment of subunits 1, 2 and 3. For all archaeal and bacterial species representatives in GTDB release 220, each subunit was identified with hmmsearch85 against the corresponding protein families (PF00115, PF00116 and PF00510) using a domain e-value cut-off of 0.001 and coverage of 50%. Subunits were concatenated if the target organism encoded (1) one copy of each subunit across its genome; or (2) multiple copies but organized one copy of each within 10 loci of each other. For organisms outside of Promethearchaeota, Cox1 was clustered with 50% sequence identity and 80% coverage using MMseqs2 easy-cluster to choose representative sets of Cox1, 2 and 3. Alignment for each subunit and tree construction of the concatenated alignment was performed as described above but with ultrafast bootstrap support (-bb 1000).

Gene expressivity was calculated using cordon56 using ribosomal proteins as a reference and the default settings. Peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of extracellular peptidases, glutamate dehydrogenases and glycine dehydrogenases with high expressivity (within the top 25% of each genome), all consistently found in isolates specialized in peptide degradation (strains MK-D1, HC1, SC1, Coprothermobacter proteolyticus, Necrotrophus endoclepta, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Salinivirga cyanobacteriivorans). Anaerobic peptidotrophy was annotated if high-expressivity OFORs and FeFe or NiFe hydrogenases were also present. Those with NiFe hydrogenase-containing gene sets homologous to those highly expressed by syntrophic Promethearchaeota isolates or archaeal electron-bifurcating hydrogenase MvhADG–HdrABC were further annotated as H2-evolving. Aerobic peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of a high-expressivity Cox (within top 50% of each genome) along with a complete complex III (cytochrome b/b6 with a cytochrome c, Rieske FeS protein and/or a copper-binding electron carrier like plastocyanin or halocyanin). Aerotolerant peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of a high-expressivity Cbd with type 1 or 2 NADH:quinone oxidoreductase but lacking the ability to transfer all electrons from peptide degradation to oxygen reduction. Different expressivity thresholds were used for peptide metabolism and terminal oxidases based on the observation that expressivity tends to be in the 25–50% range for archaea that are known to be aerobic (that is, Halobacteriales).

For prediction of aerobic capacity in Promethearchaeota genomes, classifiers were trained using a dataset of strains with annotated aerobic capacity derived from BacDive105. Strains were categorized as obligate aerobes, diazotrophic aerobes, facultative (an)aerobes and obligate anaerobes (with and without Cox). For classification, obligate aerobes, diazotrophic aerobes and facultative (an)aerobes were grouped as organisms with aerobic capacity, whereas obligate anaerobes were grouped as lacking aerobic capacity. Host-associated and phototrophic organisms (including oxygenic and anoxygenic phototrophs such as purple and green bacteria) were excluded, as host-associated oxygen gradients and light-driven metabolism can decouple oxygen exposure from intrinsic respiratory strategies, thereby confounding the relationship between genomic features and metabolic lifestyle. BacDive annotations were manually curated based on literature information and genomic annotation.

For genomic annotation, strains annotated as obligate aerobes in BacDive but encoding pathways for anaerobic respiration (that is, dissimilatory nitrate reduction or sulfate reduction) were reclassified as facultative anaerobes. Dissimilatory nitrate reduction and sulfate reduction were annotated based on the presence of genes with the following PFAM domains: Molybdopterin, Molydop_binding, Nitr_red_alph_N or NapB for dissimilatory nitrate reductases, and APS_reductase_C for adenylyl-sulfate reductase. Diazotrophy was annotated for isolates harbouring genes containing the PFAM domain Oxidored_nitro.

Strains classified as obligate anaerobes without experimental evidence of growth under aerobic conditions were excluded. Likewise, strains classified as facultative anaerobes without experimental evidence of enhanced growth under aerobic conditions were removed as they may rather be oxygen-tolerant anaerobes.

For each genome, OFOR and ODH abundance was calculated as log((n + 1)/genome size (Mb)), where n corresponds to the number of OFOR or ODH homologues. Genes encoding OFOR and ODH were annotated based on PFAM annotations generated by eggNOG-mapper (v.2.1.2)95. OFORs were identified based on the presence of PFAM domain combinations ‘POR,POR_N’, ‘PFOR_II,POR_N’, ‘POR_N,TPP_enzyme_C’ or ‘PFOR_II,TPP_enzyme_C’. OFORs containing three domains were annotated using hmmsearch and a domain e-value cutoff of 0.00001 and domain coverage cut-off of 0.8. ODH abundance was estimated based on the number of annotated E1 (decarboxylase) subunits (PFAM E1_dh), which determines the substrate specificity and serves as a proxy for the presence of 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes. Genomic frequencies were calculated for the five most discriminative amino acids reported previously61, as these capture the majority of the discriminatory signal while reducing redundancy among correlated amino acid frequencies.

Classification of aerobic capacity based on OFOR and ODH abundance or amino acid frequency was performed using LR and LDA implemented in scikit-learn (v.1.8.0). Features were standardized using z-score normalization before model training. LR was performed with balanced class weights to account for class imbalance. Models were evaluated using stratified k-fold cross-validation (StratifiedKFold; k = 5), in which the dataset was partitioned into training and test sets while preserving the proportion of organisms with and without aerobic capacity in each split. Predictions were generated using cross_val_predict, ensuring that each sample was evaluated in a held-out fold. Classification performance was assessed using accuracy and balanced accuracy based on these out-of-fold predictions. For each genome, posterior probabilities were obtained from the fitted models, and the maximum posterior probability was used as a measure of classification confidence. For Promethearchaeota, only genomes with ≥85% completeness and ≤5% contamination were analysed, with two Hodarchaeales MAGs encoding Cox and Complex I (JBSWRZ01) or Cox, Complex I and Complex III (JBSWRG01) as exceptions.

To quantify the similarity between metabolic categories, the centroid of each category was calculated as the mean of the normalized OFOR abundance and normalized ODH abundance across all genomes in that category. Pairwise distances between category centroids were first computed using Euclidean distance in the two-dimensional feature space: dij = ((xi − xj)2 + (yi − yj)2)0.5, where x and y represent the mean values of normalized OFOR abundance and normalized ODH abundance for categories i and j. These distances quantify the separation between metabolic regimes in the feature space and were visualized as a centroid distance matrix.

Moreover, Mahalanobis distances were calculated to account for the covariance structure of the data. For each pair of category centroids i and j, the Mahalanobis distance was computed as: Dij = (mui – muj)T × Σ–1 × (mui – muj), where mui and muj are the centroid vectors of the two categories and Σ is the pooled covariance matrix estimated from all genomes in the feature space.

To examine archaea specifically, ODH and OFOR abundances were also comparatively analysed for archaeal isolates. Although archaea capable of aerobic growth often use ferredoxin as an electron carrier, such organisms nearly universally conserve a unique OFOR annotatable with three PFAM domains (PFOR_II, POR_N and POR; domain e-value ≤ 0.0001 and domain coverage ≥ 80% based on hmmsearch) (334 out of 340 analysed isolates; Supplementary Table 18). The abundances of ODH and other OFORs were calculated for each archaeal isolate as described above. Promethearchaeota were compared with mesophilic archaea as, for thermophiles, increased temperature decreases oxygen solubility and may therefore influence the interaction between metabolism and oxygen.

#1413. Liverpool's anonymous attackers cost them the chance of beating Arsenal despite dominant display... the gap to the champions is narrowing - but the Reds still aren't close enough, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 21:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:06 EDT, 2 November 2026

As disheartened fans spilled out of Anfield, nearly all conversations were about the referee and questions over why he did not point to the penalty spot in the first half when Jurrien Timber pulled back Alexander Isak.

They had a point and this game would have been completely different had Andy Madley – or VAR Stuart Attwell – seen what everyone else saw when Isak was an inch short of connecting with a header and possible goal because he was pulled back by his marker.

It was a similar situation to Liverpool’s only other defeat under new boss Andoni Iraola, where supporters were left aggrieved at the incorrect call to send off Ryan Gravenberch against Manchester City.

In both cases they were unlucky to be on the wrong side of refereeing mistakes and would have cursed the fine margins. But in both cases Reds fans will also realise their team just did not do enough to win too.

Just like against City, Liverpool dominated Arsenal for large parts of this match. It felt as though they were one magic moment or opposition mistake away from scoring and lfiting off the Anfield roof.

But in both cases, that moment never materialised. It felt like the Liverpool attackers were looking around waiting for somebody else to step up and be the man to start the pendulum swinging in Liverpool’s favour.

Alexander Isak and Liverpool's attackers struggled against Arsenal's defence

They had zero shots on target, according to Opta, and that is the only statistic that Iraola will be mulling over in the coming days.

Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak have all been frighteningly good in recent weeks but in this game, especially the second half, Liverpool’s big-money forwards looked like they had run out of ideas.

Arsenal defended like their lives depended on it and their away fans, who barely saw the ball down their end of the pitch after half-time, celebrated every Gabriel header or David Raya catch like a goal.

The home team, meanwhile, were left throwing long balls forward to Virgil van Dijk – the only player who could aerially compete with Arsenal’s team of giants. It felt like several Hail Mary passes but no one could answer Iraola’s prayers.

Liverpool’s two defeats to City and now Arsenal both demonstrate the gap between Iraola’s outfit and a genuine title contender. There is definitely a small level between Liverpool and Arsenal – but Reds fans can take solace in knowing it is not a chasm like last season.

A referee decision here, a better final ball there and Liverpool may be still unbeaten under Iraola and the whole country would consider them a title contender.

Iraola has closed the gap on the top teams but knows several tweaks are still needed to take that next step. Can they do it this season? It is far from impossible but seems a tall order.

The upcoming fixture list is kinder to them, at least. Of the current top eight, Liverpool have played all of them – two in the Carabao Cup – and won each test apart from City and Arsenal. The next two league games are against teams in 18th and 17th.

Florian Wirtz has improved recently but was unable to provide cutting edge on Sunday

But right now, Liverpool are a team with too many ‘ifs’, ‘buts’ and ‘maybes’. If Alexis Mac Allister did not get under a first-half header that looked like a certain goal… if the referee had given a clear foul on Isak… if the forwards packed their shooting boots.

As it was, for all of the nail-biting moments for Mikel Arteta on the touchline as Liverpool had lots of the ball in the final third, his goalkeeper David Raya could have had a cigar in and read the papers for most of the second half.

That is what will bother Iraola the most.

As for being a complete team able to compete for the league title again, Liverpool seem so close yet so far.

Trey Nyoni made his first Premier League start and it will not be his last after he put in a solid shift.

Though he misplaced some passes and was probably lucky to escape an early yellow card after two late challenges, the 19-year-old presents Iraola with an interesting tactical quirk.

The Englishman always wants the ball and drops into the back line to start attacks, with a maturity beyond his years.

He sits deep which allows Alexis Mac Allister to play as more of a box-to-box midfielder, undoubtedly his best position.

So where does this leave Ryan Gravenberch, who spent the afternoon on the bench? Given the amount of games Liverpool have across competitions, the Dutchman will still play many minutes — but he is currently at risk of falling down the pecking order thanks to the exciting talent of Nyoni.

There is also a conversation to be had about how Liverpool’s balance and control was lost when Nyoni was replaced by Dominik Szoboszlai.

Trey Nyoni excelled for the Reds and helped the home side control the tempo

Casual football fans who maybe only tune in for the big games have never seen Wirtz play well.

They must wonder what all the fuss is about.

The German has been on fine form in recent weeks but has been like a ghost — no Halloween pun intended — in the two biggest matches against City and Arsenal.

It is all well and good performing against teams like LASK in the Champions League but Wirtz, at £116million, was signed to make a difference in these blockbuster clashes.

Instead, his national team colleague Kai Havertz continued his record of impacting the games that really matter come May. How Wirtz could do with some of that killer instinct.

#1412. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

"It's a GEM" 💎 A beautiful strike from Jérémy Doku to double Man City's lead! https://t.co/lCUFfQmdLC

There were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1411. Tottenham look set to deliver after so many disappointments but Roberto De Zerbi's side need a nasty streak if they are to build on their momentum ahead of a daunting festive period, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

By RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 06:52 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:31 EDT, 2 November 2026

It was late on Saturday evening when Roberto De Zerbi relayed a few of the comments he had shared with Tottenham’s players at half-time in their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace. One of those remarks was indicative of how quickly things can change.

In the knowledge that his side were 45 minutes away from a rare spot in the upper portion of the table, he reminded them: ‘We can't forget where we have been two weeks ago. Two weeks ago, before the Coventry game, we were last in the table and we can't forget.’

With Tottenham, it is always prudent to know calamity is never too far away, but for the first time in two years, there is a gathering excitement at the club - in the crowd and the dressing room.

The win over Palace was assisted hugely by Jean-Philippe Mateta’s red card after 13 minutes, but Spurs have an uncanny knack of slipping on the easier opportunities. Not this time – goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke punctuated a dominant performance and a third straight win. Three managers and 616 days had expired since the last such streak.

But Spurs appear to be on the march and a promising season is belatedly taking shape. To finally deliver after so many disappointments, there are certain areas where improvements must follow…

Roberto De Zerbi reminded his players of where they had come from during their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace

That was De Zerbi’s own assessment of his frontline after a familiar shortcoming against Palace may have been concealed by the win. It was not lost on him that both of Tottenham’s goals were scored by defenders, nor that they had 34 shots to Palace’s two. As ever, Spurs had abundant creativity in their side but lacked a clinical edge.

De Zerbi said: ‘If we want to follow perfection, we have to be more nasty, no? That is an individual thing, because if I'm number nine, number 10, I want to score. But I can't say nothing.’

He later clarified that comment to encompass the whole side, but it was clear that the onus falls most on Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.

In fairness to the pair, Palace defended so deep after Mateta’s dismissal that they had no space to operate, but one goal apiece this season is a poor return. Solanke, in particular, needs to do a better job of reading the movements and intentions of those around him – too often on Saturday he appeared a thought or two behind Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus, who both impressed in the more generous spaces out wide.

De Zerbi wants his side to develop a 'nasty' streak - particularly his attackers

Marmoush is an interesting case for De Zerbi. His mobility and technical ability are clear but he is yet to reveal his best position. On Saturday he was used as a No 10, having already been switched between roles on the left and up front. This experiment drew muted results.

It might be the case that a sustained run in one spot would be beneficial, but for now there appears to be confusion over where to use him. There is also a nagging thought that his best striking potential comes in a two-striker system, as shown in his most prolific period at Frankfurt, but that is not the way De Zerbi plays.

A significant improvement for Tottenham has come in midfield and, specifically, the pairing between Matheus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali.

Acquired at great cost, there was limited patience around the delivery of their impact, but time was always necessary, because De Zerbi’s system is notoriously complicated. In recent weeks, Fernandes and Tonali have shown signs that the penny has dropped on what they have to do.

This has been especially relevant in the instance of Tonali, who is very much the tempo-setter of the side on the ball and off it. On Saturday, he was excellent, or worth ‘double’ in the words of De Zerbi. There were times earlier in the season when he appeared disinterested, as if Tottenham was not the destination he had in mind, but his work rate was brilliant against Palace – he covered 12.3km, won all three of his tackles, and completed 93 per cent of his passes. He was all-action.

The same would be said for Fernandes, who covered 11.6km of ground and finessed a superb cross for Van Hecke’s goal. As a pair with Tonali, he was key to the pressing operation that limited Palace to a single counter-attack in the second half.

Mateus Fernandes (pictured) and Sandro Tonali have been huge boosts in the midfield

De Zerbi struck an interesting note after the game by alluding to the cohesiveness of his side and how it has changed on the pitch. Perhaps that relates to the recent team-bonding exercise in Marbella, but more likely they just needed time to understand the complexities of their manager’s demands.

‘I think even before the international break we were playing well,’ De Zerbi said. ‘We were playing maybe not 90 minutes, but many parts of the game we played very well. We didn't score. We conceded a stupid goal and then we lost energy. We lost spirit. We lost the right union between the players.

‘If we compare Tottenham before the international break and Tottenham after the international break, now we are playing as a team. Before the international break we were playing as many very good players, but not as a team.’

Archie Gray, for one, is getting to grips with the less familiar brief at right-back. The requirements to swap spots with Fernandes, overlap Kudus or hold the advanced position are mind-scrambling, but he has adapted well. His withdrawal at half-time against Palace was down to his first-half yellow card and doesn’t detract from a salient point – he can evidently be trusted to replace Pedro Porro, or at least give the latter scope for a breather.

Tottenham have an opportunity now. Their next four fixtures are Leeds, Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, with a nasty run waiting in December and early January.

If they can get something from Elland Road, the other three assignments present a rich opportunity for momentum before the tricky festive period.

One key area to improve in the short term will come against defensive sides who offer less space. That Spurs scored only twice from 80 per cent possession against Palace highlighted the issue.

De Zerbi said: ‘We are improving in the principle and the quality of play. Maybe we are not ready yet to play against such a low block but maybe in two or three months we will be.’
