#1409. First Anfield victory for 14 years was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Fleetwood humbling. His Arsenal look the finished article - Liverpool were authors of their own downfall, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 13:54 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:32 EDT, 2 November 2026

Five nights ago, 40 miles to the north of Anfield at a remote outpost of English football, Arsenal fell to one of the most humiliating reverses of their long and august history. In the teeth of a gale that blew in off the Irish Sea, they were knocked out of the League Cup by Fleetwood Town, a team 18th in League Two.

They left with their tails between their legs, their teenage prodigy Max Dowman sent off in a melee, their heart questioned, their quality debated, their discipline an issue. Mikel Arteta and his side knew that just a few days later, at the other end of the Fylde Coast and across the Ribble Estuary, they would have to swap running the gauntlet of the Cod Army for the challenge of facing down the roar of the Kop.

They did not shirk it. If Tuesday night was a humbling, their gritty 1-0 victory in an Anfield that was a cauldron once more felt like a significant triumph. It was a defensive masterclass from the champions, an exercise in indomitability. It was their first victory here since 2012 and it took them above Manchester City so that they sit, once more, at the top of the table. Liverpool could not summon a single shot on target.

‘It felt like the end of the world when we were knocked out at Fleetwood,’ Arteta said after this win. ‘You look so silly. I was thinking “How can I lift these players up?” You have to dig deep. This was a mission to win here and it is something that we have not done for 14 years for a variety of reasons. We knew we would have to navigate some difficult moments.’

If Arteta left Fleetwood answering questions about his management of Dowman, he finished this game by striding on to the pitch after the final whistle, pumping his fists in front of the Arsenal fans celebrating in the Anfield Road end, and beating his hand on his chest. This was a vindication for him and his team. Five nights is a long time in football.

He had talked about the harsh realities of this sport after Tuesday’s loss. He had reminded everyone that playing at this level was not like ‘Disneyland’. And this victory was not like Disneyland, either. It was less a theme park and more an assault course. It was rough and it was unforgiving and Arsenal were equal to it.

Liverpool, improving under the management of Andoni Iraola, had been talked up as title contenders ahead of this match on a dank evening on Merseyside where the streets around the ground were decorated with the toothless grimaces of rotting pumpkins on doorsteps. The home team showed exhilarating signs of their re-emergence as an attacking force.

They dominated much of the game, too, but they looked like an emerging team, a team that is still evolving. Arsenal, marshalled imperiously by Declan Rice, looked like the finished article. They created one outstanding chance and Kai Havertz converted it. That was all they needed.

Their defence stayed rock-solid, although there was some puzzlement that Liverpool were not awarded a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt-pull on Alexander Isak. After the interval, Liverpool rarely looked like drawing level.

Kai Havertz gave the Gunners a lead to defend after finishing off a well worked move early on

The German slotted home after Declan Rice fizzed a dangerous ball across the six-yard box

Winning at Anfield was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Arsenal's defeat by Fleetwood Town

The opening had been predictably frenetic. Neither team forged a chance but Trey Nyoni, who has forced his way into the first team with a series of excellent performances in midfield, could have been booked twice inside the first quarter of an hour.

The initial infringement was a nasty tackle on Martin Odegaard inside the first minute where he planted his studs in Odegaard’s ankle. The second was a spiteful tackle on Kai Havertz. Neither received a yellow card, which gave yet more pause for thought about the red card shown to Dowman at Fleetwood, and its aftermath.

Let’s get one thing straight – the criticism of Arteta for his ‘treatment’ of Dowman was absurd. It has come to something when a manager giving a player a hard stare is interpreted by some as a disproportionate response.

Nobody is necessarily hankering after a return to the days of Sir Alex Ferguson’s hairdrier or Joe Kinnear’s rants that broke records for expletives but if a boss is attracting censure because he looked at a player a bit funny, we are in big trouble.

Arteta is not there to indulge Dowman. He is there to coach him and to teach him and to help him grow up in the context of a Premier League football club. His actions in Fleetwood on Tuesday fulfilled his obligations in all of those criteria.

Arsenal survived the initial frenzy here and took the lead after 16 minutes. Liverpool were the authors of their own downfall. They gave the ball away from a goal kick, it was worked to Noni Madueke on the right, and when Madueke fed it to Declan Rice on the overlap, Rice crossed beautifully for Havertz, who touched it home at the back post.

Arsenal nearly returned the favour a minute later when they played themselves into trouble at the back. Bradley Barcola found himself through on David Raya but his first touch let him down and Rice moved across to clear the danger.

Alexis Mac Allister was left with his head in his hands after missing a glorious chance to score

Liverpool's 19-year-old talent Trey Nyoni started the match but was replaced in the second half

Liverpool recovered and began to dominate the game. Barcola’s pace began to cause Arsenal all sorts of problems down their right flank and Liverpool came close to an equaliser when Virgil van Dijk flicked on a corner and Alexander Isak was denied by the brave intervention of Raya.

Arsenal were still threatening on the counter. Christos Tzolis chipped a ball to the back post and, as Liverpool scrambled to clear it, Madueke turned it back across goal. The ball was intended for Havertz, who was unmarked in the middle, but Timber could not get out of the way of it and it bounced off him into touch.

The atmosphere was febrile. Liverpool had three appeals for penalties, first for Timber’s shirt pull on Isak, then for challenges on Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo, turned down in quick succession. Tempers began to flare on the benches.

The breathlessness of the match was relentless. Florian Wirtz drove a free kick against the face of the crossbar with Raya beaten and then, three minutes before the interval, Mac Allister ran on to a cross from Milos Kerkez and, with the goal at his mercy, directed his free header too high.

Liverpool laid siege to the Arsenal goal after the break but the openings just would not come. Isak blazed high over the bar from an angle, Wirtz had a shot on the turn blocked and then, just before the hour, Dominik Szoboszlai replaced Nyoni and, to more acclaim, Rio Ngumoha came on for Gakpo.

Still Liverpool could not prise Arsenal open. Arsenal began to grow in confidence and threat. The home team were grateful to Jeremy Jacquet for a clearance that prevented Odegaard turning Tzolis’s cross into an open goal, for Van Dijk’s brilliant interception to deny Havertz and, most of all, for a quite magnificent one-handed save from Alisson that diverted a Tzolis shot round the post. It will stand the test of time as one of the saves of the season.

Arsenal put in another excellent defensive display to frustrate and keep Liverpool at bay

Liverpool’s frustration boiled over. Mac Allister was booked for his part in an ugly fracas with Odegaard and Madueke. The stands became a mass of pointing fingers and shouts of protest and anger. Time-wasting and play-acting peppered the match. Liverpool felt the game slipping away in the angst.

Liverpool threw everything at it in the final minutes. Lewis Koumas flung himself at a bouncing ball but could not get enough power on his header, Ngumoha had a shot charged down, Barcola desperately searched for pockets of space but could not find them. There were six minutes of time added on but there was no way through. Arsenal’s defence would not yield.

#1408. Fans fume at referee Andy Madley caught laughing and joking with Arsenal stars at half-time of win at Liverpool

Published: 06:03 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 06:34 EDT, 2 November 2026

Liverpool fans are fuming after referee Andy Madley laughed and joked with Arsenal's stars at half-time of their clash on Sunday – having denied them a penalty.

The Gunners claimed their first victory at Anfield since September 2012 thanks to Kai Havertz's goal, with the win sending Mikel Arteta's side three points clear of Manchester City.

But Reds supporters came away fuming after being denied a seeming stonewall penalty in the first half when Jurrien Timber tugged back Alexander Isak.

Isak had a golden chance to equalise when he rose to meet Bradley Barcola's cross, only to miss the ball after having his shirt pulled by Timber.

The Arsenal defender avoided punishment from Madley and VAR decided against intervening despite the vehement protests of Andoni Iraola and his players.

It was therefore extra galling for Liverpool fans to see the referee appearing to tell a joke to Gabriel, Riccardo Calafiori, and Declan Rice at half-time – though of course the encounter could have been entirely innocent.

Liverpool fans are fuming after referee Andy Madley was caught laughing and joking with Arsenal's players - having denied the Reds a penalty

Liverpool were denied a penalty after Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak's shirt

Fans claim Madley shouldn't have been cracking jokes with the Premier League champions

Part of refereeing, after all, is maintaining a relationship with players.

But for Liverpool it is another twist of the knife after a painful defeat which saw them fail to score from 18 shots and left them fifth in the Premier League.

'This referee clearly had a favourite. Liverpool got robbed in broad daylight,' one fan said on X.

'At any level of the game from Sunday pub league to Premier League, referees shouldn't be laughing and joking and high-fiving players on any side. They should turn up, ref neutrally, go home,' another said.

'He should not ref any more Arsenal games,' one added.

There is no evidence that Madley is biased towards the Premier League champions.

Sky Sports pundits Jamie Carragher, Daniel Sturridge and Ian Wright unanimously agreed Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty at half-time and suggested that Isak was denied the spot-kick because he failed to make more of the incident.

Iraola thinks the game could have gone differently had Madley not missed Timber's shirt pull.

The Liverpool boss said after the match: ‘There are two situations and they are a little bit related. The Isak one is a clear penalty.

‘He's gonna head the ball in front of the goal, and they grab him where everyone sees the shirt. You don't need a lot, just to avoid Alex, because the ball just goes in front of him, and I don't see the reason why, probably because he doesn't dive or he doesn't go to the floor. It shouldn't be a reason not to concede a penalty.'

Liverpool were irate as they lost to Arsenal at home for the first time since September 2012

Iraola also pointed to a similar situation where Cody Gakpo was tugged back, but the officials said the Dutchman would not get to the ball.

‘They say the ball was too long and Cody wouldn't have arrived to the ball, but then you're basically accepting that the first one is, is a pen, no?’ added Iraola. ‘So you cannot use the argument in both ways differently. So I think it's a, yes, it's a pen, the Alex one is.’

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, the manager said: 'It's a problem we have with the game. Because he doesn't dive and go to the floor. The fact that you are even asking me if he should go to the floor, if he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100 per cent.

'It should be like this but it is what it is. Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor, otherwise they won't call it.'

Asked if he will tell Isak to do that in future, the Spaniard replied: 'Yes, definitely.'

Reds captain Virgil van Dijk took aim at VAR too after the match, expressing his disappointment at the defeat.

'I think it was a clear penalty. I've seen it back and I've seen it being given. Today it wasn't meant to be,' he said.

Asked if Isak should have reacted more, the Dutchman added: 'We have 50 cameras. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras?

'Everyone has seen it. In the end it wasn't given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal.'

Former Liverpool defender Carragher was furious that VAR had not intervened as he analysed the incident at half-time.

'One of the best goal-scorers in the league is pulled back seven yards from goal, and the pull back stops him heading the ball. Why does he need to make a meal of it? VAR, do your job,' he said bluntly.

Arsenal moved to the top of the table on 24 points with victory at Anfield, while Liverpool remained fifth after Brighton and Chelsea, who are third and fourth respectively, both won on Saturday.

Mikel Arteta hailed his side’s resilience to win at Anfield.

Asked if it feels better to do so as a player or manager, he said: ‘Now it feels better as a manager, it has been such a long time without this feeling. We are extremely proud, especially the conditions we arrived in after the defeat against Fleetwood looked like the end of the world.

‘But then you have to pick yourself up. Four days later you have to come to Anfield against this manager and this team.’

#1407. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE

In a flash the balance of play shifted in Newcastle’s favour. They poured forward in search of the equaliser. Jaissle switched to a 4-4-2 with Will Osula joining Fernandez-Pardo up front, but instead of pulling level, Coventry pulled further ahead.

"We need to improve the things we can control, and right now that's a lot" 🗣️ Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle expresses his disappointment after his side's loss to Coventry 👇 https://t.co/fatJkZYyRM

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. We know we are going to have to suffer this season, when we don’t have a lot of the ball. We have to understand it. The level is what it is.

The work ethic, the belief. You get what you deserve. Great finishes. We haven’t quite had the rub of the green this season and that might have helped us nick a couple of more points. I’m a firm believer that you keep going. It was a complete performance. We’ve got to keep our feet on the ground because we’re going to have to do 30+ of those but it’s a great feeling for the players.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1406. Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes1,2. However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8+ T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8+ T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8+ T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8+ T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have substantially improved the prognosis and survival of patients with various solid cancers3, including melanoma4,5,6, non-small cell lung cancer7,8 and bladder cancer9,10,11. However, the overall response rate remains around 30%, which leaves many patients without clinical benefit12. The mechanisms that underlie this heterogeneous response remain poorly understood, which limits the ability to predict and improve ICI efficacy in individual patients.

Recent advances in immunotherapy suggest that the tumour stroma has a pivotal role in shaping responses to ICIs, functioning both as a facilitator and a barrier to effective antitumour immunity1,2. Diverse stromal components engage in continuous reciprocal communication with tumour cells to influence tumour progression and therapeutic responses. A major challenge in defining how the tumour stroma shapes ICI responses is the lack of experimental systems that accurately recapitulate these dynamic, multicellular interactions with high human relevance. Recent advances, including patient-derived xenografts13,14,15, humanized mouse models16,17,18 and ex vivo culture of human tumour tissues using air–liquid interface (ALI) techniques19,20, have improved the representation of human tumour architecture and complexity. However, precise manipulation and tracking of individual cell types and their interactions in these systems are challenging, which limits detailed mechanistic analyses of tumour–stroma–immune crosstalk.

In this study, we developed patient-derived, combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids from individuals with renal cell carcinoma (RCC). These assembloids recapitulate dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells and reflect patient-specific responses to immunotherapy. By integrating genetically manipulated assembloids with humanized mouse models, we identified a signalling axis that governs tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk and the mechanisms that underlie differential responses to ICIs. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into heterogeneous ICI responses and establish a platform for developing strategies to enhance immunotherapeutic efficacy across diverse malignancies.

To investigate the cellular and molecular basis of heterogeneous ICI responses in RCC, we established patient-specific tumour assembloids21 that faithfully recapitulate therapeutic responses by reconstituting autologous tumour cells, CAFs and tumour-infiltrating immune (TII) cells from RCC tissue samples (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Pretreatment tumour tissue samples from six patients before ICI therapy were used to generate tumour organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 1). Organoids from all patients were successfully propagated; however, with prolonged culture, cells negative for carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9−) progressively dominated, an effect that is probably due to in vitro growth advantages (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To overcome this technical difficulty, CA9+ and CA9− cells were isolated and separately maintained as distinct organoid populations (Extended Data Fig. 1d). The resulting CA9+ organoids contained canonical clear-cell RCC-associated somatic alterations, including VHL mutations and other recurrent driver events, whereas no detectable VHL mutations were identified in the CA9− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1e–h and Supplementary Data 2). Both populations maintained clear-cell histology with distinct morphological and immunohistological features (Extended Data Fig. 1d).

Next, we generated patient-specific RCC assembloids by reconstituting CA9+ and CA9− populations with patient-matched CAFs and TII cells at ratios reflecting the cellular composition of the corresponding primary tumours. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Patient-derived CAFs and TII cells were isolated and expanded separately (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), a process that largely preserved their major cellular compositions relative to the corresponding parental tumours. CAFs exhibited a phenotype similar to myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) and comparable proportions of cells expressing key markers (Extended Data Fig. 2a–e). Conversely, TII cells preserved the overall composition of major immune cell populations despite modest shifts in specific subpopulations in some patients (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c).

To characterize assembloid formation over time, we performed time-course analyses at days 0, 3, 5 and 7. Cultures were initiated from dissociated single cells at day 0, and no organized tissue architecture was evident up to day 3 (Fig. 1a,b). Multicellular organization emerged by day 5, and by day 7, the assembloids recapitulated key structural and histological features of the matched parental tumours. In detail, tumour cells were associated with CAFs and were infiltrated by immune cells while maintaining >90% cell viability throughout the culture period (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). The assembloids also retained the genetic alterations of the parental tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Extended Data Fig. 4d–i and Supplementary Data 3).

a,b, Representative immunofluorescence (a) and haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained (b) images from a time-course analysis of patient-derived RCC assembloid formation in comparison to corresponding parental tumours from six patients (P-1 to P-6). Scale bars, 100 μm. c, Heatmap showing pairwise similarity between RCC assembloids (A) and their corresponding parental tumours (T) based on somatic mutation profiles. d, Proportion of shared and unique mutations in each patient-derived pair. e, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots showing major cell populations identified by scRNA-seq in RCC assembloids and corresponding parental tumours from six patients. f, Dot plots showing the expression of selected marker genes for each cell type. g, Cell-type composition of RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. h, Pairwise comparison of cell-type proportions between RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours for each patient pair. i, Cell-type-specific transcriptomic similarity between RCC assembloids and their matched parental tumours. Detailed methods for these analyses are provided in the Methods. j, Representative immunofluorescence images of RCC assembloids treated with isotype control IgG or anti-PD-1. Scale bars, 100 µm. k,l, Quantification of cleaved caspase-3+ cells (k) and the proportion of cleaved caspase-3+ cells (l) in the indicated cell types following IgG or anti-PD-1 treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids per group were analysed, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). m, Summary of the clinical responses of patients with RCC to ICI therapy and corresponding responses in assembloids to anti-PD-1. Statistics: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction (g) or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (k,l); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (k,l). HVGs, highly variable genes; R, responder; NR, non-responder; NED, no evidence of disease; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.

We also performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of RCC assembloids and directly compared them with the corresponding parental tumour datasets at single-cell resolution. Through integrated analysis, we identified the major tumour microenvironment (TME) compartments in both RCC assembloids and parental tumours, including tumour cells, CAFs and diverse immune populations (Fig. 1e,f). Although cell-type proportions varied across patients, assembloids and matched parental tumours showed overall concordance in tumour, stromal and immune cell composition (Fig. 1g,h). Moreover, cell-type-specific transcriptomic comparisons revealed high similarity between assembloids and their matched parental tumours across multiple cell types (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 4j–o).

Notably, all patient-specific RCC assembloids faithfully recapitulated the therapeutic responses of their corresponding patients to ICIs. Treatment of RCC assembloids with anti-PD-1 antibodies for 7 days induced substantial tumour reduction and increased apoptosis in four patient-derived assembloids (P-1, P-4, P-5 and P-6). This result was confirmed through cleaved caspase-3 staining in tumour cells, and by the minimal apoptosis observed in CAFs and immune cells (Fig. 1j–l). By contrast, assembloids from two patients (P-2 and P-3) did not exhibit significant tumour cell death (Fig. 1j–l). The responses of individual assembloids to anti-PD-1 mirrored the clinical outcomes of the corresponding patients from which the assembloids were generated (Fig. 1m). Together, these findings establish that patient-specific RCC assembloids generated from autologous tumour cells, CAFs and immune cells are a robust experimental platform that recapitulates the histopathology and ICI responsiveness of parental tumours in the cohort analysed.

We next sought to investigate the mechanisms that underlie differential ICI responses in RCC. Assembloids established from responders contained a significantly higher proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells (TIM3−TCF1+) relative to exhausted and differentiated cells (TIM3+TCF1−)22,23,24,25,26 than assembloids developed from non-responders (Fig. 2a). This result was consistent with the patterns observed in matched parental tumour tissue samples (Fig. 2b). Notably, depletion of stem-like CD8+ T cells markedly impaired anti-PD-1 responsiveness and tumour cell killing (Extended Data Fig. 5a), which indicated that these cells are required for effective anti-PD-1 responses23,24,27,28,29,30,31,32.

a,b, Top, flow cytometry analyses (left) and quantification (right) of stem-like T cells in RCC assembloids (a) and parental tumours (b) from responders and non-responders. Bottom, expression profiles of exhaustion and effector markers in terminally differentiated (TD) and stem-like (Stem) T cell subsets from P-2. For a, three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per patient (n = 3); for b, three biologically independent samples were analysed per patient (n = 3). c, Flow cytometry analyses of stem-like T cells in four mix-and-match RCC assembloids (A–D) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Blue, responder; red, non-responder. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (A, n = 48; B, n = 24; C, n = 24; D, n = 12). d, Flow cytometry analyses of the proportion of stem-like T cells in combinatorial RCC assembloids from responders. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). e, Anti-PD-1 responses in combinatorial RCC assembloids from responders. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 µm. f–i, Top, schematic of the experiment. Bottom, flow cytometry plots and bar graphs show the proportion of stem-like T  cells. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). f, RCC assembloids lacking tumour cells and CAFs were cultured for 7 days in the presence of tumour-CM and CAF-CM. g, RCC assembloids lacking CAFs were cultured for 7 days in the presence of CAF-CM. h, RCC assembloids lacking tumour cells were cultured for 7 days in the presence of tumour-CM. i, CAFs and TII cells were cultured in a Transwell system, with CAFs in the bottom chamber treated with tumour-CM and TII cells cultured in the top Transwell insert. Statistics: two-tailed nested t-test (a,b), one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (c,d) or two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (e–i); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (a–i).

To determine whether T cell stemness is intrinsically programmed or maintained via non-T cell-autonomous mechanisms, we generated mix-and-match assembloids by reconstituting responder-derived and non-responder-derived TII cells with tumour cells and CAFs from the opposite group (Extended Data Fig. 5b). CD8+ T cells retained stemness only when combined with responder-derived tumour cells and CAFs, whereas non-responder-derived environments did not preserve T cell stemness (Fig. 2c). This result suggests that T cell stemness is maintained in a non-T cell-autonomous manner. To define the cellular components responsible for this effect, we generated combinatorial assembloids that lacked TII cells, tumour cells or CAFs (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Assembloids reconstituted with all three components from responder tumours preserved stem-like CD8+ T cells, whereas removal of either tumour cells or CAFs markedly reduced T cell stemness (Fig. 2d). Only assembloids containing all three components from responder tumours showed substantial tumour cell reduction following anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 2e). This finding demonstrates that both tumour cells and CAFs are required for maintaining T cell stemness and therapeutic responsiveness. Furthermore, lineage-tracing experiments showed that stem-like CD8+ T cells were primarily maintained through the expansion of pre-existing stem-like cells rather than de novo conversion (Extended Data Fig. 5d–f).

We next designed four experimental conditions using combinatorial assembloids to investigate how tumour cells and CAFs cooperate to maintain T cell stemness in responders (Fig. 2f–i and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Assembloids lacking both tumour cells and CAFs did not expand stem-like T cells, even when cultured with conditioned media (CM) from tumour cells (tumour-CM) or CAFs (CAF-CM) (Fig. 2f). This finding indicated that direct communication between tumour cells and CAFs is required. Notably, CAF-CM alone did not restore T cell stemness in CAF-deficient assembloids, whereas tumour-CM restored stem-like T cell frequencies in tumour-deficient assembloids to levels comparable to controls (Fig. 2g,h). These results suggest that tumour-derived soluble factors activate CAFs to produce stemness-supportive factors. Moreover, tumour-activated CAFs maintained T cell stemness through soluble factors. That is, when responder-derived CAFs were cultured in tumour-CM, stem-like T cells were preserved even without direct contact (Fig. 2i). Together, these findings provide support for a tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell signalling axis in which tumour cells induce CAFs to secrete stemness-supportive factors. This process preserves stem-like CD8+ T cells in a non-T cell-autonomous manner to induce effective anti-PD-1 responses.

Comparative transcriptome analysis of CAFs from assembloids generated from responders and reconstituted with or without patient-matched tumour cells (Extended Data Fig. 5h,i) revealed 245 highly upregulated genes. Among these, we focused on seven genes that encode secreted proteins with potential roles in cell–cell communication (Extended Data Fig. 5i and Supplementary Data 5). Gene expression analyses of patient-derived CAFs showed that FGF2 and INHBA (which encodes activin-βA chain (also known as inhibin-βA chain)) were highly and consistently upregulated across all samples (Fig. 3a).

We generated genetically manipulated RCC assembloids by reconstituting patient-matched tumour cells and TII cells with responder-derived CAFs in which either FGF2 or INHBA was individually knocked down (Fig. 3b). INHBA knockdown (KD) abolished the maintenance of stem-like CD8+ T cells, whereas FGF2 KD had no significant effect (Fig. 3c). Moreover, assembloids containing CAFs with INHBA KD did not exhibit tumour reduction following anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 5j). These findings indicate that activin A is a tumour-induced, CAF-derived effector that sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and is required for effective anti-PD-1 responses in RCC (Extended Data Fig. 5k–n).

We next investigated the tumour-cell-derived ligands responsible for INHBA induction (Extended Data Fig. 5o). RNA-seq of responder-derived tumour cells revealed 9,141 expressed genes (Extended Data Fig. 5p and Supplementary Data 6), of which 205 candidate genes were identified by regulatory potential scoring33 (Extended Data Fig. 5p and Supplementary Data 6). Intercellular communication analysis34 further revealed 14 signalling pathways and 37 predicted ligands with tumour-to-CAF signalling potential (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5q). Analyses of freshly isolated tumour cells from responders identified three consistently expressed candidate factors: SEMA3B, TNF and WNT2B (Fig. 3g).

We therefore generated RCC assembloids containing responder-derived tumour cells with individual KD of SEMA3B, TNF or WNT2B, together with patient-matched CAFs and TII cells (Fig. 3h). WNT2B KD substantially reduced INHBA expression in CAFs and stem-like T cell populations across responders, whereas SEMA3B or TNF KD had minimal or no effect (Fig. 3i,j). Notably, assembloids containing WNT2B KD tumour cells did not respond to anti-PD-1 therapy. Specifically, they did not show significant tumour reduction compared with isotype controls (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 5r). These results demonstrate that tumour-derived WNT2B induces activin A expression in CAFs, which in turn sustains stem-like CD8+ T cells and promotes therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 in RCC.

To investigate why non-responders do not have this signalling axis, we performed comparative transcriptomic profiling of tumour cells and CAFs from responders and non-responders (Extended Data Fig. 5s and Supplementary Data 7 and 8). The tumour cells displayed highly comparable transcriptomic landscapes between the two groups (Fig. 4a), with similar WNT2B expression (Fig. 4b). CAFs likewise showed largely similar transcriptomic profiles and predominantly myCAF features35,36 (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 5t); however, CAFs from non-responders exhibited markedly reduced INHBA expression (Fig. 4d). Notably, INHBA expression in CAFs from non-responders was not restored even when reconstituted with tumour cells from responders (Extended Data Fig. 5u,v). This result suggests that there is an intrinsic defect in the response of these CAFs to tumoural WNT signals. Indeed, mix-and-match assembloids containing responder-derived tumour cells and TII cells with non-responder CAFs showed poor responses to anti-PD-1 treatments (Extended Data Fig. 5w). Thus, resistance in non-responders is associated with a CAF-intrinsic defect in responding to tumour-derived WNT2B rather than an intrinsic difference in tumour cells. In support of this idea, CAFs from non-responders showed reduced canonical WNT–β-catenin target gene expression and deficient WNT pathway activation (Fig. 4e,f). Together, these findings demonstrate that impaired WNT responsiveness in CAFs is a substantial barrier to anti-PD-1 efficacy in RCC.

To pinpoint the molecular basis of WNT unresponsiveness in CAFs from non-responders, we analysed WNT-pathway-associated genes and identified 61 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between responders and non-responders (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Data 8). Comparisons of 16 key WNT pathway regulators revealed 3 candidate genes of particular interest: FZD1, FZD6 and LRP6 (Supplementary Data 8). Analyses of freshly isolated CAFs showed that LRP6 expression was substantially reduced in non-responders (Fig. 4h).

We genetically engineered CAFs from non-responders to express LRP6 and reconstituted them with patient-matched tumour cells and TII cells (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 5x). LRP6 restoration reinstated INHBA and WNT target gene expression, restored the stem-like CD8+ T cell population and rescued anti-PD-1 responsiveness (Fig. 4i–k). Together, these findings indicate that there is a distinct subset of LRP6-deficient, WNT-unresponsive CAFs enriched in non-responders. Owing to a lack of activin A expression, these CAFs fail to sustain CD8+ T cell stemness and contribute to resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy (Extended Data Fig. 5y,z).

We next investigated the tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk identified in RCC assembloids using two additional experimental platforms: patient-specific in vivo humanized mice37,38,39 and ex vivo ALI organoids19,20 (Fig. 4l). In the humanized mouse model, RCC assembloids containing patient-derived tumour cells together with autologous CAFs were orthotopically transplanted under the kidney capsule of NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Patient-matched peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were then intravenously infused to reconstitute a human immune cell population, a process that achieved around 10% CD8+ T cells among human CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c).

Anti-PD-1 extensively reduced tumour burden in mice transplanted with control tumours. By contrast, mice transplanted with responder tumours in which WNT2B was knocked down exhibited substantially blunted anti-PD-1 responses, which was accompanied by a reduction in the stem-like CD8+ T cell population without affecting overall immune cell infiltration, including CD8+ T cells (Fig. 4m and Extended Data Fig. 6d–i). For mice transplanted with tumours from a non-responder, tumours containing INHBA-expressing CAFs showed robust anti-PD-1 responses with significantly reduced tumour weight compared with IgG controls, along with increased stem-like CD8+ T cell populations. By contrast, mice transplanted with tumours with control CAFs remained resistant to treatment, despite comparable immune cell infiltration levels (Fig. 4m and Extended Data Fig. 6j–n).

We further examined the tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk using previously established ALI organoids19,20. WNT pathway inhibition in ALI organoids developed from a responder abolished the anti-PD-1-mediated reduction in tumour cells observed in control organoids (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 6o–r). Conversely, supplementation with recombinant activin A restored anti-PD-1 sensitivity and resulted in a substantial decrease in tumour burden relative to IgG-treated controls in ALI organoids generated from a non-responder (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 6o,s–u).

Together, these patient-specific humanized mouse and ALI organoid models, combined with genetic and pharmacological manipulations, demonstrate the pivotal role of the WNT–activin A–T cell stemness axis across multiple patient-relevant platforms. The data also highlight the robustness and translational significance of tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk in shaping anti-PD-1 responses.

We analysed scRNA-seq datasets from the pretreatment RCC tissue samples used to generate the RCC assembloids (Fig. 5a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Data 4). We identified 24 clusters representing the major TME compartments, including epithelial tumour cells, CAFs, endothelial cells, macrophages, CD8+ T cells and other immune cell subpopulations (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). Overall, the proportions of these major cell types were similar between responders and non-responders (Extended Data Fig. 7d).
