a, Schematic of patient-specific RCC assembloid generation. CA9+ and CA9− cells, CAFs and TII cells were isolated from pretreatment RCC tissues, reconstituted at patient-matched ratios and cultured on a shaker for 7 days. Histopathology, mutational profiles, cellular composition and transcriptomic profiles of assembloids were compared with those of the corresponding parental tumours. Assembloids were then treated with anti-PD-1, and in vitro responses were compared with each patient’s clinical outcome to ICI therapy. b, Schematic workflow for the establishment and maintenance of RCC-derived cultures. For tumour cells, dissociated single-cell suspensions were separated into CA9+ and CA9− populations, each embedded in Matrigel to generate and maintain CA9+ and CA9− organoids, respectively. CAFs were isolated as adherent spindle-shaped cells and expanded in adherent culture. TII cells were maintained and expanded in suspension/adherent culture. c, Representative immunofluorescence images of RCC organoids established without separating CA9+ and CA9− cells at an early stage of culture (top) and maintained in prolonged culture (bottom). Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. d, Representative immunofluorescence images of CA9+ (top) and CA9− (bottom) RCC organoids, with corresponding H&E staining. Scale bars, 100 µm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. e, Oncoplot showing somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. f, Relative fractions of six base substitution types identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. g, Variant-class composition of somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations. h, TMB in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. CR, complete response; NED, no evidence of disease; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.

a, Representative immunofluorescence images of patient-derived CAFs. Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. b, Gating strategy for the analysis of CAFs. c, Flow cytometry plots of primary CAFs from RCC tissues (top) and cultured CAFs (bottom). Three technical replicates were analysed per group (n = 3). d, Heatmaps showing the relative expression of representative myCAF, iCAF and apCAF marker genes in primary and cultured CAFs derived from six RCC patients, as assessed by RT–qPCR. Three technical replicates were analysed per group (n = 3). e, Pearson correlation analysis of gene expression profiles between primary and cultured CAFs for each patient shown in panel d. Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (c); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c).

a, Representative immunofluorescence images of patient-derived TII cells. Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. b, Gating strategy for the analysis of immune cell populations. c, Flow cytometry plots of primary TII cells from RCC tissues (top) and cultured TII cells (bottom). Three biologically independent samples were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (c); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c).

a, Gating strategy used for the analysis of RCC assembloid viability over time. b, Flow cytometry plots showing the proportion of live cells in RCC assembloids from six patients at days 0, 3, 5 and 7 following assembloid formation. Live cells were identified as FVD506-negative cells. c, Quantification of the proportion of live cells in RCC assembloids from six patients at days 0, 3, 5 and 7 following assembloid formation. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed for each time point (n = 3). d, Oncoplot showing the mutational status of a curated panel of genes frequently mutated in RCC, identified by whole-exome sequencing of parental tumours (P-1 to P-6). e, Hierarchical clustering based on TMB, base substitution patterns and variant-class composition. f, TMB in parental tumours and RCC assembloids. g, Relative fractions of six base substitution types in parental tumours and RCC assembloids. h, Variant-class composition of parental tumours and RCC assembloids. i, Proportions of CA9+ and CA9− cells in patient-specific RCC assembloids. j–l, Transcriptomic similarity between parental tumours and RCC assembloids across all 36 parental tumour–assembloid combinations from six patients. Similarity was assessed using HVGs (j), patient DEGs (k) and tumour signatures (l). Detailed methods for these analyses are provided in the Methods. m, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative RCC tumour-cell marker genes in tumour cells from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. n, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative CAF subtype marker genes in CAFs from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. o, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative immune cell subtype marker genes in immune cells from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. Data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c,i). A, RCC assembloids; T, parental tumours.

a, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids following depletion of stem-like CD8+ T cells. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. b, Experimental design for mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Tumour cells and CAFs from either responders or non-responders were reconstituted with TII cells from either responders or non-responders, as indicated, generating four combinatorial RCC assembloid groups. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days and analysed by flow cytometry. c, Experimental design for combinatorial RCC assembloids. RCC assembloids were generated by selectively removing specific cell populations and cultured for 7 days. These assembloids were used to assess T cell stemness and anti-PD-1 responses. d, Experimental scheme illustrating lineage-tracing analysis of stem-like and non-stem-like CD8+ T cells in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Stem-like (SLAMF6+) and non-stem-like (SLAMF6−) CD8+ T cells were sorted based on SLAMF6 expression and labelled with CellTrace CFSE or CellTrace Blue, respectively, prior to reconstitution into RCC assembloids. e, Flow cytometry gating strategy used for sorting stem-like (SLAMF6+) and non-stem-like (SLAMF6−) CD8+ T cells for lineage-tracing analysis in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. f, Representative flow cytometry plots and quantification of lineage-tracing analysis in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). g, Schematic illustration of three proposed hypotheses for tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell interactions in maintaining stem-like T cells. Experimental conditions and corresponding results are shown in Fig. 2f–i. h, Schematic workflow for identifying CAF-derived factors involved in stem-like T cell maintenance. CAFs were isolated from RCC assembloids, and comparative transcriptome analysis along with secreted factor profiling was performed to identify candidate genes, which were subsequently validated in functional assays. i, Transcriptomes of control CAFs and CAFs reconstituted with patient-matched tumour cells from responders were compared. Differential expression analysis identified 586 genes upregulated in the reconstituted CAFs (P < 0.05), of which 245 were highly expressed (average expression > 2). Limiting this set to genes encoding secreted proteins further narrowed the list to seven final candidates. j, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of INHBA KD in CAFs from responders on anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids. CAFs were transduced with INHBA shRNA lentiviruses, reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by anti-PD-1 response analysis. k, Schematic diagram to assess the effects of stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs. l, Representative fluorescence image showing microinjection of CellTrace CFSE-labelled stem-like CD8+ T cells into RCC assembloids. Scale bar, 100 μm. m, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs following stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation, with or without activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. n, Proportion of stem-like T cells in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs following stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation, with or without activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). o, Schematic workflow for identifying tumour cell–derived factors that induce INHBA expression in CAFs. Tumour cells were isolated from RCC assembloids of responders after 7 days of culture. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes expressed in tumour cells (expression level > 0.4), filtered for those positively correlated with INHBA expression in CAFs and predicted to have tumour–CAF communication potential. Candidate genes were subsequently validated in functional assays. p, Experimental strategy to identify tumour-derived ligands that drive activin A (INHBA) expression in CAFs. Bulk RNA-seq of responder cells (CA9+ and CA9−) yielded 9,141 genes with detectable expression. Using NicheNet’s ligand-to-target matrix, we ranked ligands and retained those with positive regulatory potential for INHBA (687 genes), then intersected across samples to obtain 205 ligands with consistent positive potential. Candidate ligands were next evaluated for tumour–CAF signalling using CellChat on the tumour/CAF transcriptomes, which highlighted 14 tumour-to-CAF signalling families; filtering to ligands participating in these pathways produced 37 candidates with tumour–CAF communication potential. q, The 37 candidate ligands expressed in responder tumour cells, grouped by signalling family. r, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of WNT2B KD in tumour cells from responders on anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids. Tumour cells were transduced with WNT2B shRNA lentiviruses, reconstituted with CAFs and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by anti-PD-1 response analysis. s, Schematic workflow for comparative transcriptomic analysis of tumour cells and CAFs from responders and non-responders to investigate mechanisms underlying the anti-PD-1 resistance in non-responders. t, Heatmap showing expression of canonical marker genes for CAF subtypes, analysed by RNA-seq. u, Experimental design of mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Tumour cells and TII cells from responders were reconstituted with CAFs from non-responders, and vice versa, to generate mix-and-match RCC assembloids. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days and subsequently analysed for gene expression and anti-PD-1 responses. v, Relative expression of INHBA in CAFs from mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). w, Anti-PD-1 responses in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Four biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 12). Scale bars, 100 μm. x, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of LRP6 expression in CAFs from non-responders in RCC assembloids. CAFs were transduced with lentivirus containing LRP6 cDNA, reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by gene expression and anti-PD-1 response analysis. y, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids from non-responders reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells in the absence of CAFs following activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. z, Proportion of stem-like T cells in RCC assembloids from non-responders reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells in the absence of CAFs following activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (a,w,z), two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (m,y), one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (n) or two-tailed nested t-test (v); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (a,f,m,n,v,w,y,z). Ctrl, control; αPD1, anti-PD-1.

a, Experimental design for assessing anti-PD-1 responses in humanized mice. WNT2B KD tumour cells from a responder (P-1) or INHBA-expressing CAFs from a non-responder (P-2) were reconstituted with patient-matched CAFs or tumour cells, respectively, and orthotopically transplanted into NSG mice, followed by PBMC infusion and IgG or anti-PD-1 treatment. b, Gating strategy for PBMCs from humanized mice. c, Flow cytometry plots showing human immune cells in PBMCs from humanized mice from a responder (P-1) and a non-responder (P-2). hCD45+ cells were analysed for hCD3+ T cells, hCD19+ B cells, hCD14+ monocytes, hCD4+ T cells and hCD8+ T cells. Five mice were analysed per group (n = 5). d,j, Representative H&E and immunofluorescence images of parental tumours and tumours from humanized mice from a responder (P-1, d) and a non-responder (P-2, j), with quantification of CD45+ and CD8+ cell infiltration (top) and the proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells (bottom). Four biologically independent samples were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per sample (n = 12). e,k, Proportion of CD8+ T cells among infiltrating immune cells. Four mice were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per mouse (n = 12). f,l, Relative expression of WNT2B and INHBA in tumours containing control or WNT2B KD tumour cells (f) and control or INHBA-expressing CAFs (l). Three mice were analysed per group (n = 3). g,m, Representative H&E images of responder-derived tumours (P-1, g) and non-responder-derived tumours (P-2, m) in humanized mice shown in Fig. 4m. Tumour area (mm²) was measured in five H&E-stained sections at 1-mm intervals per kidney, with the mean representing one biological replicate. Four mice were analysed per group (n = 4). Scale bars, 100 μm. h, Gating strategy for tumour-infiltrating human immune cells from xenotransplanted tumours. i,n, Proportion of stem-like T cells in humanized mice from a responder (P-1, i) and a non-responder (P-2, n). Three mice were analysed per group (n = 3). o, Experimental design for assessing anti-PD-1 responses in ALI organoids. Responder organoids (P-5, left) were treated with IWR-1 and non-responder organoids (P-3, right) with recombinant activin A, followed by IgG or anti-PD-1 treatment. p,s, Representative H&E and immunofluorescence images of parental tumours and ALI organoids derived from a responder (P-5, p) and a non-responder (P-3, s), with quantification of CD45+ and CD8+ cell infiltration (top) and the proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells (bottom). Four biologically independent samples were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per sample (n = 12). Scale bars, 100 μm. q,t, Proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells. Four biologically independent organoids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per organoid (n = 12). r,u, Relative expression of WNT2B and INHBA in ALI organoids treated with control or IWR-1 (r) and control or recombinant activin A (u). Three biologically independent organoids were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (d–f,i–l,n,p–u) or two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (g,m); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c–g,i–n,p–u).

a, UMAP plots of scRNA-seq data from pretreatment RCC tissues of six patients (P-1, P-4, P-5, P-6: responders; P-2, P-3: non-responders). b, Dot plots showing the expression of selected marker genes for each cluster. c, Feature plots of representative marker genes used to define each cell type. d, Violin plots showing the proportions of major cell types in RCC tumour tissues from responders (R, n = 4) and non-responders (NR, n = 2). e, Feature plots showing the expression patterns of WNT genes in tumour cell clusters. f, Violin plots of representative marker genes for myCAFs, iCAFs and apCAFs, stratified by INHBAhigh and INHBAlow CAFs from RCC patients (n = 6). g, Violin plot showing INHBA expression levels in CAFs from individual patients (n = 6). Statistics: two-tailed Welch’s t-test (d) or two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (g). For box plots (f,g), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range.

a, Schematic workflow for scRNA-seq of pretreatment tumour tissues from responders (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 and R6) and non-responders (NR1 and NR2). b, UMAP plots showing major cell populations identified in RCC patients (n = 8). c, Dot plots showing the expression of selected marker genes for each cluster. d, Bar graph showing the relative proportions of cell types in individual patients. e, UMAP plot (left) and violin plot (right) showing WNT2B expression levels in tumour cells from individual patients. f, Feature plots showing the expression patterns of WNT ligand genes in tumour cell clusters. g, Correlation of average CAF gene expression profiles between responders and non-responders. h, Dot plot showing expression of canonical marker genes for CAF subtypes. i, UMAP plots of CAFs from responders (R) and non-responders (NR). j, Proportion of INHBAhigh CAFs in responders and non-responders. k, Violin plots of representative marker genes for myCAFs, iCAFs and apCAFs, stratified by INHBAhigh and INHBAlow CAFs from RCC patients (n = 8). l, Violin plots showing expression of INHBA and LRP6 in CAFs from RCC patients (n = 8) stratified by INHBA expression status. m, Violin plot showing INHBA expression levels in CAFs from individual patients. n, Violin plots showing expression of LRP6 in CAF subclusters. o, GSEA of INHBAhigh versus INHBAlow CAFs showing enrichment of the WNT signalling pathway in INHBAhigh CAFs. p, Violin plots showing expression of the stem-like T cell signature in CD8+ T cells from responders (R, n = 6) and non-responders (NR, n = 2). q, Schematic workflow of spatial transcriptomic analysis of pretreatment RCC tissues from one responder and one non-responder, using publicly available Visium datasets obtained from GEO (GSM641570540 for the responder; GSM592403841 for the non-responder). r,s, Left, spatial maps of transcriptional clusters overlaid on tissue sections from the responder (r) and the non-responder (s). Right, corresponding spatial feature plots showing cell type–specific gene signatures. t, Representative spatial transcriptomic maps from a responder and a non-responder, showing WNT2B+ tumour spots, TCF7+ CD8+ T cell spots, LRP6+ myCAF spots and LRP6+INHBA+ myCAF spots, alongside H&E-stained images and spatial feature plots of cell type marker genes. u, Violin plots showing WNT2B expression in tumour spots from responders and non-responders. v, Box plots quantifying the number of CAF spots adjacent to WNT2B+ tumour spots in RCC patients (n = 2). w, Box plots depicting spatial relationships between WNT2B+ tumour spots, CAF spots and TCF7+ CD8+ T cell spots in RCC patients (n = 2). x, GSEA of CAF spots adjacent to WNT2B+ tumour spots between one responder and one non-responder. y, Schematic workflow of spatial transcriptomic analysis performed on pretreatment RCC tissues from an independent cohort of six patients (three responders, three non-responders) using GeoMx DSP. z, Representative GeoMx DSP ROI images from responders (case1–3) and non-responders (case4–6). Tumour and myCAF regions were identified by PanCK (green) and αSMA (red) staining, respectively. ROIs designated for sequencing of tumour and myCAF regions are indicated. aa–gg, Comparative transcriptomic analyses of tumour and myCAF regions in responders versus non-responders. aa, Linear similarity in tumour (PanCK+) regions. bb, PCC heatmap showing transcriptional similarities of tumours across individual responders and non-responders. cc, WNT2B expression in tumour (PanCK+) regions in RCC patients (n = 6). dd, Linear similarity of myCAF (αSMA+) profiles between responders and non-responders. ee, PCC heatmap showing transcriptional similarities of myCAFs across individual responders and non-responders. ff, INHBA expression in myCAF (αSMA+) regions in RCC patients (n = 6). gg, Pathway enrichment analysis of myCAFs based on upregulated DEGs in responders, demonstrating enrichment of WNT signalling–associated pathways. Statistics: two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (d), two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (e,l–n,p,v–x), unpaired two-tailed t-test (cc,ff) or one-sided Fisher’s exact test, with FDR correction for multiple comparisons (gg). For box plots (k–n,p,v,w), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Data show the mean ± s.e.m. (cc,ff).

a, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy across four solid tumour types (gastric, lung, ovarian and prostate cancers) using TCGA bulk RNA-seq datasets. Tumours with enriched WNT expression were selected, and target patient subsets were subsequently stratified into two groups based on T cell stemness signatures, INHBA expression and LRP6 expression. b, Identification of target patient subsets in gastric cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer. Patient ranking plots are shown based on WNT expression, hot tumour signatures and CAF-associated signatures. c, Proportion of target patients identified in each cancer type from TCGA bulk RNA-seq datasets. Target patients were defined based on enrichment of WNT expression together with hot tumour and CAF-associated signatures. d, Left, heatmaps showing T cell stemness signature, INHBA expression, LRP6 expression and WNT expression in target patients identified by k-means clustering. Right, box plots comparing T cell stemness signature, INHBA expression, LRP6 expression and WNT expression between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 169; lung cancer, n = 622; ovarian cancer, n = 127; prostate cancer, n = 108). e, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy used to analyse bulk RNA-seq datasets from ICI-treated patients across three solid tumour types (gastric, lung and ovarian cancers). Patient subsets exhibiting enriched WNT expression were identified, and correlations among immunotherapy responses, INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness signature and WNT expression were subsequently analysed. f, Identification of target patient subsets in gastric, lung and ovarian cancers. Patient ranking plots are shown based on WNT expression. g, Transcriptomic analyses of ICI-treated cohorts from gastric, lung and ovarian cancers. Top, heatmaps showing integrated joint scores for INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness signature and WNT expression in the analysed patient cohorts. Bottom, box plots comparing responders (R) and non-responders (NR) with respect to integrated INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness scores and WNT expression (gastric cancer, n = 70; lung cancer, n = 83; ovarian cancer, n = 38). h, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy used to analyse scRNA-seq datasets across four solid tumour types (gastric, lung, ovarian and prostate cancers). Patient subsets harbouring WNT-expressing tumours were identified, and cell-type-specific expression of WNT, INHBA and LRP6, as well as correlations among the proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells, the proportion of INHBA+LRP6+ CAFs and tumoural WNT expression, were subsequently analysed. Patients lacking detectable CAF or CD8+ T cell populations were excluded from downstream analyses. i, UMAP plots showing major cell populations identified by scRNA-seq in gastric cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer. j, Heatmaps showing representative marker gene expression patterns across major cell populations within each cancer type. k, Feature plots (left) and patient ranking plots (right) showing tumour WNT expression in individual patients from each cancer type. Patients harbouring WNT-expressing tumour cells were selected for downstream analyses. l, Heatmaps showing the proportions of INHBA- and LRP6-expressing cells across major cell populations within each cancer type. m, Top, heatmaps showing the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+ and/or LRP6+ CAFs across target patient subsets identified by clustering analyses. Two patient groups were stratified based on the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+ and/or LRP6+ CAFs. Bottom, box plots comparing the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+/LRP6+ CAFs between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 19; lung cancer, n = 27; ovarian cancer, n = 8; prostate cancer, n = 9). n, Left, heatmaps showing WNT expression in tumour cells across target patient subsets identified by clustering analyses. Right, box plots comparing tumoural WNT expression between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 19; lung cancer, n = 27; ovarian cancer, n = 8; prostate cancer, n = 9). Statistics: two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (d,m,n) or two-tailed Welch’s t-test for WNT expression and the one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test for integrated joint scores (g). For box plots (d,g,m,n), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range.

In this study, we identified dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells that determine tumour responses to ICIs in human RCC. CAF-derived activin A promotes the maintenance and expansion of the TCF1+ stem-like CD8+ T cell pool in inflamed tumours, thereby establishing a responding hot tumour state. In this setting, tumour-derived WNT2B induces activin A production in LRP6-positive CAFs, which in turn sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and drives expansion of the stem-like T cell pool. By contrast, when activin A expression is minimal or absent in inflamed settings due to the presence of tumour-adjacent LRP6-deficient CAFs, it fails to sustain CD8+ T cell stemness, resulting in non-responding hot tumours and resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy.

#1405. Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and - if that fails - punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 18:05 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:37 EDT, 2 November 2026

Football’s lawmakers like to meddle. The problem is they do it in areas that tend not to need any meddling. Like around handball and offside and other places that were doing just fine as they were.

So here’s a tip for the meddlers at the International Football Association Board. Meddle somewhere that needs it. Meddle in a way that would be meaningful and important and in a way that would actually help the game.

Please meddle with cheating. Please do something that would spare us from the embarrassment of grown men behaving like children in a bid to get other players booked and sent off. Yes, please meddle there.

Because football at the top level really needs it.

It needs a route through which players such as Alexis Mac Allister and Gabriel Magalhaes can be properly punished, shamed and embarrassed for what they did during Sunday’s otherwise fabulous Premier League game between Liverpool and Arsenal at Anfield.

It needs a deterrent. It needs greater power to match referees and greater leeway for retrospective punishment.

Alexis Mac Allister drops to the floor holding his face after his forehead is slightly brushed

The Liverpool man tried to get Noni Madueke sent off during Arsenal's 1-0 victory at Anfield

In a way, it is handy that there was one from each team this time. That way, we can be spared the usual accusations of bias that tend to come when footballers are called out for their sins.

Here, live on TV, Gabriel and Mac Allister were both as bad as each other. One in each half, clear as day.

Arsenal defender Gabriel was poked in the chest early on by Aleksandar Isak and went down holding his face. Then, much later, Liverpool’s Mac Allister was brushed by the forehead of Noni Madueke and did likewise.

Neither fooled referee Andy Madley. Both were told to get up and get on with the game. On TV, Sky Sports analysts Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher didn’t hold back.

‘Embarrassing’ was the word they both chose. Neville to describe Gabriel and Carragher as a way of calling out Mac Allister.

But this type of chicanery is more than that. We see it from lots of players and we see it all the time. It’s not just embarrassing. It goes much deeper. It’s malevolent. It’s low. It’s pre-meditated. It’s wicked.

Short of dark subjects such as spitting and leg-breaking tackles, I can’t think of much worse things on a football field than pretending to have a head or facial injury when you actually haven’t.

So where IFAB need to get involved – where they need to ‘meddle’ – is simple. They must increase football’s powers to punish.

On the field and in the moment, referees can issue yellow cards for simulation and for cheating. Players can be booked for exaggerating contact (Mac Allister) or pretending contact has been made with a certain area of the body when it hasn’t (Gabriel).

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes performed a similar act of cheating in the first half

The Brazilian fell down clutching his face after Alexander Isak brushed his neck and chest

But why is there no power – at least in occasional and exceptional circumstances - to issue a red card?

Gabriel and Mac Allister appeared to be trying to get their opponents sent off. Would they do it if they knew the match referee at least had the option of showing them the red card instead?

Retrospectively, meanwhile, we need greater leeway for action.

Under a law passed a decade ago, a player can theoretically be banned by a review panel for two-games for ‘successful deception of a match official’. However the reality is that the initiative has largely been superseded by VAR and was only really used for players diving to try and win penalties anyway.

In terms of the nonsense we witnessed at Anfield on Sunday – and indeed see on a reasonably regular basis around the country – there is very little recourse once the game is over so once again a possible deterrent has been removed from the equation.

Cheating of this nature currently looks and feels like a risk worth taking and that is what must change.

Alexander Isak was not given a penalty despite being blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber

Here, it was interesting to hear Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola suggest afterwards that he must start telling his players to go down under contact. He was talking about Isak’s refusal to buckle under a clear penalty area shirt tug from Jurrien Timber.

That’s an important issue, too. Players should not be punished for their honesty. A foul is a foul, regardless of the reaction. VAR should have awarded a penalty.

But here on an otherwise fine day for the Premier League, another known and rather ugly blot on the landscape grew larger.

The threat of red cards for cheating and – if that fails - punishments handed down by review. That’s the kind of meddling we should all be on board with.

#1404. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

Tonight’s hosts are yet to qualify for a major tournament and are expected to set up in a defensive shape. England defender Esme Morgan believes the squad are ready for a long night of breaking down a stubborn opposition.

She told a pre-match press conference: “It’s just about persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. A really good example was the away game against Ukraine in qualifying. We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1403. Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature

Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions3,4,5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Emotion regulation is a core determinant of mental and physical health1. It encompasses the strategies that people use, intentionally or automatically, to influence their emotional experience. Among these, cognitive reappraisal—changing the interpretation of a situation to alter its emotional impact—has received particular attention in psychology, psychiatry and the broader public. It is central to cognitive-behavioural therapy and linked to resilience, lower symptom burden and improved daily affect1.

Neuroimaging studies have extensively mapped the neural basis of reappraisal. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) consistently implicates a network of lateral and medial prefrontal regions, often along with reduced amygdala activation during reappraisal of negative stimuli2. These findings have informed neuromodulatory interventions for emotion regulation deficits6,7,8. Still, they are based primarily on within-person designs that contrast experimental conditions such as ‘reappraise’ versus ‘view without regulation’ in the same individuals, and many studies and broader theories extend these neural within-person mechanisms to explain between-person individual differences in well-being or psychopathology4,5. This extension is not necessarily warranted.

Extending within-person neural mechanisms to explain between-person differences risks the ecological fallacy9: associations at one level need not hold at the other. For instance, people who habitually use reappraisal report better well-being than others. However, in daily life, reappraisal often occurs in response to stressors and may therefore coincide with worse-than-average momentary mood.

Compounding this, prefrontal regions that are engaged during reappraisal also participate in working memory, response selection and pain processing10—limiting their specificity as emotion-related markers of regulatory function. Task designs, moreover, may not mirror naturalistic regulation, raising questions about ecological validity and relevance for individual-difference research11,12. A recent systematic review found partial effect convergence in prefrontal and amygdala circuits, but studies were underpowered13 (median n = 25) and too heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis3. In turn, meta-analyses on reappraisal in mental disorders have yielded mixed results, with inconsistent findings in the prefrontal cortex4,14,15.

To resolve this, we conducted a preregistered consortium analysis of 40 fMRI datasets on the neurobiology of emotion regulation capacity (NIDER consortium; n = 2,175;  Methods, ‘Consortium procedures’ and Supplementary Table 1)—approximately 20 times larger than previous efforts3—with sufficient power to detect even small between-person associations (r = 0.10; Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’). In this context, reappraisal capacity refers to individual differences in whether, and how effectively, people use reappraisal to reduce negative affect. We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal. Prior work has linked these three indices with each other and with prefrontal activity during reappraisal3,16,17,18,19. To our knowledge, this assumption has not been tested at scale. Notably, the most widely used trait questionnaires are generally understood to index self-reported habitual tendencies to reappraise rather than the ability to implement reappraisal. We nonetheless included them given their proposed functional link to such ability16,17,18 and their widespread use.

We explored whether the three indices converge on a shared core, and whether any of them relate to activity in canonical emotion regulation circuits during common reappraisal tasks2. Our findings have direct implications for neuromodulatory interventions, biomarker development and the validity of individual-difference research in affective neuroscience.

In a first step, we aimed to assess the overlap between the three main indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation. If these three indices represent a similar core construct, or are otherwise functionally related, they should show a meaningful association. Individual consortium study teams calculated the correlations between the three indices of reappraisal capacity based on a standardized coding protocol using functionally predefined regions of interest, ensuring that higher values on each index indicate higher reappraisal capacity. Study-level results were aggregated with random-effects meta-analyses, which is statistically equivalent to person-level random-effects mega-analysis for the preregistered analyses and was intended to circumvent data sharing thresholds (Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’). The evidence for null results was further quantified using Bayes factors (Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’).

There was a statistically significant association between amygdala down-regulation and task-based affective ratings (P = 0.010; Table 1 and Forest plots in Extended Data Figs. 1–3). As hypothesized, participants with stronger down-regulation of the amygdala via cognitive reappraisal showed a better down-regulation of task-based affective ratings. Yet, the effect size was comparatively small (r = 0.08): To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80%, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

There was no significant association between trait questionnaires and either outcome—that is, amygdala down-regulation or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.06, BF10 ≤ 0.16; Table 1). Confidence intervals ruled out even small effect sizes (r = 0.10), for which statistical power was above 88% given the maximal observed between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; Supplementary Fig. 1). The overlap (shared variance) between the three indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity is shown in Fig. 1, which indicates no shared overlap between all three. Bayes factors substantially favoured the null hypothesis for associations with trait questionnaires (BF10 ≤ 0.16). Between-study heterogeneity was not statistically significant in any of the three tests (P > 0.17) and was particularly small for the non-significant correlations (τ = 0.00 and 0.06), indicating that these null findings are unlikely to be explained by differences in study design.

Pairwise overlap between three widely used indices of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation. Overlap is shown as shared variance derived from the corresponding pairwise random-effects meta-analytic Pearson correlations, which are displayed next to each intersection. The correlations were: task-based affective ratings with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.08, P = 0.010, k = 26, n = 1,377; trait questionnaires with task-based affective ratings, r = 0.05, P = 0.067, k = 28, n = 1,397; and trait questionnaires with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.01, P = 0.807, k = 33, n = 1,833. All tests were two-sided and uncorrected.

All studies made use of trait questionnaires that primarily assess beliefs about habitual reappraisal use. Although relations to implementation ability, as measured by experiments, are theoretically and empirically expected16,17,18, trait questionnaires that directly measure beliefs about such abilities might show stronger associations. To test this, we performed a subsequent analysis based on three large studies that additionally administered modified versions of the emotion regulation questionnaire to capture such beliefs about abilities20. Fixed-effects meta-analysis confirmed that beliefs about habitual use and implementation ability are strongly related (r = 0.67; Table 1). Supporting the null results for habit questionnaires, there was substantial evidence against an association between these ability trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings (BF10 = 0.13). By contrast, the association between trait ability questionnaires and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant (P = 0.010), but in the opposite direction, meaning that beliefs in higher reappraisal capacity were related to less effective down-regulation of the amygdala. This represents strong evidence against an effect in the expected direction (one-sided BF10 = 0.05).

To address the second research question, we examined whether individual differences in the three reappraisal indices were systematically related to neural activity during cognitive reappraisal beyond the amygdala. We first tested these associations in canonical emotion regulation networks derived from prior meta-analytic work2 (Fig. 2a) and then complemented these confirmatory analyses with exploratory whole-brain analyses, both outlined in the preregistration (Methods, ‘Statistical analyses’). This strategy was intended to assess whether the three indices showed associations with established regulatory circuitries and whether any observed effects converged on overlapping or distinct neural regions.

Significant associations are shown at the whole-brain level after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q < 0.05, two-sided). All significant effects were negative. The shared colour bar indicates Pearson’s r, with more intense colours reflecting stronger negative correlations. The colour bar was truncated at −0.30 for visibility reasons, although larger negative correlations were frequent for amygdala down-regulation (d). There was no statistically significant association between trait questionnaires and neural activity during reappraisal (Fig. 2b). The correlations with average activity in the two predefined networks were negligibly small and the null hypothesis strongly favoured by Bayes factors (both |r| ≤ 0.03, P > 0.25, uncorrected, BF10 < 0.02; k = 37, n = 2,091). No voxels survived the correction for multiple comparisons in the voxel-wise networks of interest or the whole-brain approach. All brain-wide effect sizes were smaller than |r| = 0.11 (mean = −0.01, range −0.10 to 0.09).

These null results were stable when using a jackknife procedure—that is, no statistically significant voxels when repeating the meta-analysis while leaving out one study at a time. They were further supported by Bayesian posterior odds for voxels across the canonical emotion regulation networks2 (that is, Bayes factors corrected for multiple comparisons; Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’). The null hypothesis was decisively favoured for 98% of voxels with odds over 100:1, there were no voxels with favourable odds for the existence of an effect, and only two voxels favoured the null in an ambiguous range below 3:1. The power to detect a small effect (r = 0.10) was 96% for average network responses (τ = 0.07). Power in voxel-wise analyses was mostly above 80% in simulated scenarios for this effect size, especially for the network of interest approach (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

As in the previous section, a fixed-effects meta-analysis of three studies that provided trait questionnaires specifically targeting beliefs about ability yielded no statistically significant results (both a priori networks |r| < 0.04, P > 0.511, BF10 < 0.07, uncorrected; k = 3, n = 444). No voxels survived thresholding; all Bayesian posterior odds favoured the null hypothesis (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.25).

As for trait questionnaires, there was no statistically significant association between average down-regulation of task-based affective ratings and average neural activity during reappraisal in the preregistered regulatory networks, with strong support for the null hypothesis by Bayes factors (both |r| < 0.03, P > 0.22, BF10 < 0.03, uncorrected; k = 31, n = 1,958). No voxels within these networks survived correction for multiple comparisons in voxel-wise analyses.

Within canonical emotion regulation networks2, about 98% of voxels showed null effects that were decisively supported by Bayesian posterior odds (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.29), with only 12 voxels falling into an indecisive range (mean = 0.84, range 0.34 to 2.52). By contrast, five voxels in the brainstem (caudal pons) provided substantial evidence for an effect (mean = 7.31, range 4.84 to 13.89). Using uncorrected Bayesian posterior odds, evidence for effects was observed in 55 voxels exceeding 3:1 odds, including the amygdala (mean = 69.63, range 3.02 to 1,055.27). This pattern aligns with the uncorrected preregistered findings from the amygdala region-of-interest analyses (see ‘Divergence of capacity indices’).

For whole-brain analyses, the jackknife procedure indicated that results were highly sensitive to the inclusion of data from Brehl et al.21 (Extended Data Fig. 4), potentially owing to its large sample size in combination with study-specific effects (for example, data were collected in the context of the first COVID-19 outbreak). In the full analysis, a negative association with task-based affective ratings was observed in a cluster of 86 voxels outside the canonical regulatory networks. Excluding data from Brehl et al.21 increased the extent of significant voxels substantially to 587, mainly in sensorimotor and dorsal attention regions, with smaller clusters in visual cortex, caudate nucleus and brainstem (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Table 1). Across these regions, better down-regulation of negative emotions was associated with lower activation (mean = −0.11, range −0.16 to −0.09). Together, these results suggest that classically emotion-generating regions, but not emotion-regulating regions, are indicative of emotion regulation capacity, albeit with small effect sizes.

To facilitate the psychological interpretation of the significant neural activation pattern, we conducted automated meta-analytic decoding using Neurosynth, which quantifies the association between whole-brain activation maps and large-scale term-based meta-analytic patterns derived from the neuroimaging literature (for example, ‘pain’, ‘fear’ and ‘motoric’). Neurosynth decoding against 50 topic maps from 11,406 fMRI studies indicated that the meta-analytic activation map is most similar to language processing (‘comprehension’: r = 0.17, ‘sentence’: r = 0.16 and ‘semantic’: r = 0.14) and most dissimilar to sensorimotor processing, consistent with the deactivation observed in whole-brain analyses (‘hand’: r = −0.25, ‘movements’: r = −0.22, ‘motor’: r = −0.17).

Top-down theoretical models predict that effective reappraisal should be associated with lower amygdala and higher prefrontal responses—an opposing pattern. Between-person differences in overall brain responsivity12,22, however, could blur such regional specificity.

Contrary to theoretical predictions, participants with stronger amygdala responses during reappraisal also showed substantially stronger responses throughout the rest of the brain in the same contrast (mean r = 0.27, range −0.08 to 0.68; Extended Data Fig. 5; correlation signs are reversed in the figures because amygdala down-regulation was coded as [view negative − reappraise negative]). This included both regulatory networks (first: r = 0.29, P < 0.001; second: r = 0.24, P < 0.001; k = 35, n = 2,088) and more than 170,000 voxels brain-wide, with only a single voxel showing a negative correlation (Fig. 2d). A person with a larger amygdala response than others, therefore, also tends to show larger responses in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and elsewhere—making the expected opposing pattern almost undetectable with standard fMRI individual-difference analyses.

This pattern was not unique to the amygdala. For all pairs among 489 anatomical regions23 (Methods, ‘Inter-region correlations’) in an independent reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33), any two brain regions were on average highly correlated across participants (r = 0.58, s.d. = 0.18).This means that individuals who respond more strongly in one region tend to respond more strongly everywhere across the brain, compared with other people. Crucially, this was not specific to reappraisal: the same pattern held across 18 studies spanning negative emotion, pain and cognitive control10 (mean r = 0.37; Fig. 3a), with between-person correlations among canonical resting-state network responses25 reaching 0.50–0.80 (Fig. 3b). Person-level whole-brain responsivity thus potentially reflects pervasive confounding processes for regional fMRI inference—an issue that affects not only reappraisal research, but also the broader task-based individual-difference literature.

a, Between-person correlations (that is, across participants) of regional activation across pairs of brain regions in an independent multimodal task–fMRI dataset spanning three domains—cognitive control, negative emotion and pain processing—with three subdomains per domain and two studies per subdomain (n = 15 per study; total n = 270). Each dot shows the mean Pearson correlation across all possible pairs of 489 regions; whiskers indicate the s.d. across region pairs. b, Between-person Pearson correlations of activation profiles between pairs of resting-state networks in the same dataset, additionally including a reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33). Colours encode the magnitude of Pearson’s r, and the top row shows the mean across studies. Networks were defined using the Yeo parcellation25. Rows show individual studies; columns show network pairs. dAttention and vAttention denote dorsal and ventral attention networks, respectively; Default denotes the default mode network.

These profound individual differences in global signal responses are in conflict with the argument that most fMRI tasks have been designed to elicit strong within-person effects, at the cost of meaningful between-person variance, despite their common use in individual-difference research26. We tested this potential misalignment by analysing trial-wise responses to negative pictures in two large samples with population-representative variance in negative emotional dispositions, using the most common reappraisal task12 (Methods, ‘Variance decomposition’). For trial-wise task-based affective ratings, the majority of variance was at the within-person level (92–93%; Fig. 4). By contrast, for neural responses in the amygdala and regulatory networks, about 60% of variance was on the between-person level. Thus, associations are likely to be reduced because common fMRI task designs prioritize robust within-person condition effects over between-person effects26, a mismatch that is further amplified by large individual differences in global signal responses.

Variance decomposition for three focal outcomes—task-based affective ratings, amygdala responses and regulatory network responses—in two large task–fMRI studies50 (the Pittsburgh Imaging Project (PIP) (study 1) n = 176, and Adult Health and Behavior Project, phase 2 (AHAB-2) (study 2) n = 180; Supplementary Table 1). Bars show the proportion of total variance attributable to between-person and within-person variability. Single-trial responses were extracted for each outcome and decomposed using intercept-only linear mixed-effects models, with the random intercept indexing between-person variance and the residual term indexing within-person variance. To obtain stable estimates, trial-level responses outside three times the interquartile range were removed within each participant, followed by removal of participants whose average responses fell outside three times the interquartile range. Between-person variance estimates were low for task-based affective ratings but substantially higher for amygdala and regulatory network responses. Exact proportions of total variance attributable to between-person differences were as follows. Study 1: ratings 0.07, 95% confidence interval [0.05, 0.09]; amygdala 0.64, 95% confidence interval [0.59, 0.69]; regulatory network 0.62, 95% confidence interval [0.57, 0.66]. Study 2: ratings 0.08, 95% confidence interval [0.06, 0.10]; amygdala 0.60, 95% confidence interval [0.55, 0.65]; regulatory network 0.56, 95% confidence interval [0.51, 0.61].

Finally, we tested whether multivariate neural signatures provide more sensitive indices of reappraisal capacity than anatomically defined regions or networks. Neural signatures are predictive decoding models that combine activity across many brain regions to estimate the presence or intensity of a psychological state in new individuals. We focused on three established candidate signatures: a negative affect decoder, a decoder of reappraisal as a dynamic state, and a decoder trained to predict individual differences in reappraisal success from task-based affective ratings (Methods, ‘Multivariate neuro-affective signatures’).

Using the four largest studies (n = 730), we first examined whether these signatures differentiated emotion generation from reappraisal (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Table 2). The negative affect decoder was strongly expressed during emotion generation (d = 0.69) but increased further during reappraisal (d = 0.15), indicating that its expression did not follow the expected reappraisal-related reduction in negative affect. The reappraisal state decoder showed stronger negative expression during emotion generation (d = −0.41) than positive expression during reappraisal (d = 0.30), suggesting limited specificity for reappraisal as opposed to variation in emotional state. The reappraisal ability decoder showed substantial negative expression across both contrasts (d = −0.22 for emotion generation and d = −0.37 for emotion regulation). Consistent with these ambiguous task-response profiles and univariate null findings, none of the three signatures was significantly associated with reappraisal capacity, whether indexed by trait questionnaires or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.08; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Table 3). Descriptive correlations were near-zero (|r| ≤ 0.06), with confidence intervals excluding effects larger than |r| = 0.15 and Bayes factors favouring the null hypothesis (BF10 < 0.25), especially for the negative affect decoder (BF10 < 0.09).

a, Responses of neural signatures, the amygdala and the regulatory network to the two main contrasts: emotion generation [view negative – view neutral] and emotion regulation (reappraise negative – view negative). Metrics are expressed as Cohen’s d. Smaller points indicate study-specific estimates; larger points and error bars indicate estimates aggregated across studies and their 95% confidence intervals (uncorrected, two-sided). Total n = 730; study 1 n = 180 (AHAB-250), study 2 n = 176 (PIP50), study 3 n = 139 (Doren et al., unpublished) and study 4 n = 235 (ref. 21). The negative affect decoder was not used in study 1, and the reappraisal ability decoder was not used in study 2 to avoid inflated effect sizes, as these were the training samples for the previously published decoders.
